# How to use this guide

Pharmaceutics is the biggest first-year D.Pharm subject (75 theory hours). The syllabus has 7 chapters; chapter 5 (dosage forms) alone has about 41 hours, so in this guide it is split into three units (4, 5 and 6). Study one unit every two or three days: read the notes, draw every diagram once from memory, learn the tables, and then answer the question bank without looking.

| Guide unit | Syllabus chapter | Hours in syllabus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. History of pharmacy and pharmacopoeias | 1 | 7 |
| 2. Packaging materials and pharmaceutical aids | 2 and 3 | 5 + 3 |
| 3. Unit operations | 4 | 9 |
| 4. Tablets and capsules | 5 | 8 + 4 |
| 5. Liquid oral, topical, nasal and ear preparations | 5 | 6 + 8 + 2 |
| 6. Powders, granules, sterile and immunological products | 5 | 3 + 6 + 4 |
| 7. Manufacturing plant, QC, QA and cGMP | 6 | 5 |
| 8. Novel drug delivery systems | 7 | 5 |

## Exam pattern (ER-2020 theory paper)

D.Pharm ER-2020 exams are yearly. In Himachal Pradesh the board (HPTSB) conducts them under the PCI ER-2020 regulations. The theory paper is **80 marks, 3 hours**; another 20 marks come from sessional (internal) assessment. The usual ER-2020 board paper looks like this. Confirm the exact split with your college, because boards sometimes change the format.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | Objective questions (MCQs / one-word / fill in the blanks) – all compulsory | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| II | Short answers – attempt 10 of 11 | 10 × 3 = 30 |
| III | Long answers – attempt 6 of 7 | 6 × 5 = 30 |

In this guide the **long** questions are 5-mark answers and the **short** questions are 3-mark answers, to match this pattern. A few **very-short** (2-mark) questions are included for quick revision and for sessional tests.

## Probability ratings

- **High** – asked in most years; prepare the full answer with diagrams and tables.
- **Medium** – asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** – rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

Ratings are an estimate from the syllabus weight and the kind of questions usually set in D.Pharm papers. They are not a promise.

## Scoring tips for Pharmaceutics

1. **Start with a definition.** Every answer – tablet, emulsion, validation, insufflation – should begin with a clear one- or two-line definition.
2. **Draw the equipment.** For hammer mill, ball mill, cyclone separator, fluidized bed dryer and triple roller mill, a labelled diagram earns marks. Then write principle → construction → working → uses → merits and demerits.
3. **Use tables for comparisons:** o/w vs w/o emulsion, flocculated vs deflocculated suspension, QC vs QA, liniments vs lotions, sugar vs film coating, types of glass.
4. **Quote official numbers correctly:** disintegration times, weight variation limits, friability (not more than 1%), simple syrup 66.7% w/w, 0.9% NaCl isotonic, autoclave 121 °C for 15 minutes.
5. **Give examples.** Name at least one real preparation for every type (Calamine Lotion, Turpentine Liniment, Lugol's solution, Ocusert, nitroglycerin patch).
6. **For a 5-mark long answer**, aim for about one and a half pages: definition, classification/table, diagram, 4–5 points of explanation, advantages and disadvantages.
7. **For a 3-mark short answer**, write 5–6 crisp points or a small table; do not write an essay.
8. Practical knowledge helps: questions on emulsions, suspensions, effervescent granules and injections often ask for a formula or method you prepared in the laboratory.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you have only a few hours, learn these topics with full diagrams and tables: **tablet granulation, defects and evaluation**, **emulsions (types, tests, preparation, stability)**, **suspensions (flocculation, Stokes' law)**, **hammer mill, ball mill and fluidized bed dryer**, **freeze drying**, **types of glass and plastics problems**, **preservatives**, **injections and their QC tests**, **vaccines, toxoids and sera**, **QC vs QA, cGMP, validation**, and **NDDS classification**.

## Dates and names (Unit 1)

| Fact | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Chopra Committee (Drugs Enquiry Committee) | 1930–31 |
| Drugs (and Cosmetics) Act | 1940 |
| Pharmacy Act / PCI set up | 1948 / 1949 |
| First Indian Pharmacopoeia / latest | 1955 / 2022 (IP Commission, Ghaziabad) |
| BP / USP / NF first editions | 1864 / 1820 / 1888 |
| Father of pharmacy education in India | Prof. M. L. Schroff (BHU, 1932) |
| Extra Pharmacopoeia | Martindale (reference, not official standards) |

## Packaging and aids (Unit 2)

| Item | Key point |
| --- | --- |
| Type I / II / III / NP glass | Borosilicate / treated soda-lime / soda-lime / non-parenteral |
| Amber glass | Protects light-sensitive drugs |
| Plastic problems | Permeation, leaching, sorption, chemical reaction, modification |
| Rubber problem | Sorbs preservatives → pre-soak closures in preservative |

| Saccharin, aspartame, sucralose | About 300–500×, 200×, 600× sucrose |
| Preservatives | Benzoates (acid pH), parabens, chlorocresol 0.1%, phenol 0.5%, benzalkonium 0.01% (eye) |
| Antioxidants | BHA, BHT, tocopherol (oil); ascorbic acid, metabisulphite (water); EDTA synergist |

## Unit operations (Unit 3)

| Equipment | Principle | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hammer mill | Impact | Milling granules, crude drugs |
| Ball mill | Impact + attrition; best at 1/2–2/3 of critical speed | Fine grinding, wet or dry |
| Cyclone separator | Centrifugal force | Separating solids from air |
| Double cone blender | Tumbling | Dry powder blending |
| Turbine mixer | High-speed impeller | Liquids |
| Triple roller mill | Shear between rollers at different speeds | Ointments, pastes |
| Silverson | Rotor–stator high shear | Emulsions, creams |
| Membrane filter | Sieving; 0.22 µm sterilises | Sterile filtration |
| Sintered glass filter | Fused glass particles; grades 1–5 | Corrosive liquids; grade 5 holds bacteria |
| Fluidized bed dryer | Hot air suspends granules | Fast drying of granules |
| Freeze dryer | Sublimation below triple point | Heat-sensitive biologicals |

IP powder grades: coarse 10/44, moderately coarse 22/60, moderately fine 44/85, fine 85, very fine 120.
Extraction: infusion, decoction, digestion, maceration (7 days), percolation, Soxhlet; solvent = menstruum, residue = marc.

## Tablets and capsules (Unit 4)

| Test | Limit |
| --- | --- |
| Weight variation (IP) | ≤80 mg ±10%; 80–250 mg ±7.5%; ≥250 mg ±5% (20 tablets; ≤2 outside, none at double) |
| Disintegration | Uncoated 15 min, film 30 min, sugar 60 min, dispersible 3 min; enteric: intact 2 h in 0.1 M HCl, then 60 min in pH 6.8 |
| Friability | 25 rpm, 100 revolutions; loss ≤1% |
| Hardness | About 4–6 kg |
| Dissolution | 900 ml, 37 ± 0.5 °C; basket 100 rpm, paddle 50 rpm |
| Capsule weight variation | <300 mg ±10%; ≥300 mg ±7.5% |
| Capsule disintegration | 30 min |

Defects: capping/lamination (air, fines, dry granules), picking/sticking (moisture, low lubricant), mottling (colour migration). Sugar coating: seal → subcoat → smooth → colour → polish → print. Capsule sizes 000 (largest) → 5; softgels by rotary die with plasticiser (glycerin).

## Liquids and topicals (Unit 5)

- Simple syrup 66.7% w/w (IP); elixir = sweet hydroalcoholic.
- Emulsion primary ratio (oil : water : gum): fixed 4:2:1, volatile 2:2:1, mineral 3:2:1.
- o/w dilutes with water and conducts; w/o does not.
- Creaming reversible, cracking irreversible; Stokes: v = 2r²(ρ1 − ρ2)g / 9η.
- Flocculated: fast settling, loose sediment, no cake.
- Ointment bases: oleaginous, absorption, emulsion (w/o, o/w), water-soluble (PEG).
- Liniment with rubbing; lotion without rubbing; paste = high solids.
- Suppository bases: theobroma oil (melts 30–35 °C, polymorphism), glycerinated gelatin, PEG; displacement value.

## Powders, sterile and immunological (Unit 6)

- Insufflation = powder blown into cavities; sterile dusting powder for wounds.
- Effervescent granules: citric : tartaric 1 : 2; fusion uses citric acid's water of crystallisation.
- Injections: sterile, pyrogen-free, particle-free, isotonic (0.9% NaCl, 5% dextrose; −0.52 °C).
- Sterilisation: autoclave 121 °C/15 min; dry heat 160 °C/2 h; filtration 0.22 µm; ethylene oxide; gamma rays.
- QC: sterility (thioglycollate, soybean–casein digest), pyrogen (rabbit), endotoxin (LAL), leakage (dye), clarity.
- Eye drops sterile, isotonic, preserved; discard 4 weeks after opening.
- Vaccines = active immunity (live, killed, toxoid, subunit); sera = passive immunity (horse antitoxins, ASV).
- Toxoid = toxin + formaldehyde, adsorbed on aluminium salts; store vaccines 2–8 °C, never freeze adsorbed vaccines.

## Plant, QC, QA (Unit 7)

- Schedule M = GMP in India. One-way flow; sterile Grades A–D.
- QC = testing (product, reactive); QA = all systems (process, proactive). QA ⊃ GMP ⊃ QC.
- Calibration = instrument vs standard; validation = documented evidence of consistent results.
- Validation types: prospective, concurrent, retrospective, revalidation; DQ, IQ, OQ, PQ.

## NDDS (Unit 8)

- Aim: control rate, duration or site of release; steady levels.
- Examples: OROS (osmotic), transdermal patches (nitroglycerin, nicotine, fentanyl, scopolamine), Ocusert (pilocarpine), levonorgestrel implant/IUD, liposomal amphotericin B.
- Challenges: cost, dose dumping, fixed dose, toxicity cannot be stopped quickly.

# Handling and referring to official references

**Aim:** To learn how to use official references (pharmacopoeias, formularies and reference books) to find formulas, standards, methods and procedures for preparing and testing dosage forms.

> Use the editions available in your college library (for example IP 2018 or IP 2022, BP, Martindale, National Formulary of India). Handle the books carefully and return them to the shelf.

## Principle

Every official preparation has a **monograph** that gives its formula or composition, method of preparation (where given), tests and storage. The **general notices** explain the words used, and the **appendices / general chapters** give the official test methods. A pharmacist must be able to find this information quickly and correctly.

## Requirements

Indian Pharmacopoeia (current edition), British Pharmacopoeia, Martindale (Extra Pharmacopoeia), National Formulary of India, BPC (older formulas), practical record book.

## Procedure

1. Note the edition, year, publisher and number of volumes of each book.
2. Read the **general notices** of the IP and write the meaning of: "about", "constant weight", storage terms (cool place, room temperature), solubility terms (very soluble … practically insoluble).
3. Use the **index** to find a monograph, for example *Paracetamol Tablets*. Write down: definition and content limits, identification, tests (uniformity of weight, dissolution, related substances), assay, storage and labelling.
4. Open the **appendix** for one test (for example disintegration test) and write the apparatus, conditions and limits.
5. From a formulary or BPC, copy the official master formula of one preparation (for example Calamine Lotion) and convert it into a **working formula** for 50 ml or 100 ml.
6. In Martindale, look up one drug and note: uses, dose, adverse effects, interactions and two proprietary names.
7. Record each search in a table.

## Observations

| Reference | Item searched | Information found | Page / section |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| IP | Paracetamol Tablets | Content limits, tests, storage | |
| IP appendix | Disintegration test | Apparatus, 37 ± 2 °C, time limits | |
| Formulary / BPC | Calamine Lotion | Master formula | |
| Martindale | Paracetamol | Uses, dose, adverse effects | |

**Working formula calculation**

```text
Working quantity = (Master quantity × Quantity required) ÷ Master formula quantity
Example: Calamine 15 g per 100 ml → for 50 ml: 15 × 50 ÷ 100 = 7.5 g
```

## Result

Official references were studied and information on the given monographs, test methods and formulas was retrieved and recorded.

## Precautions

1. Always use the current official edition for standards.
2. Copy numbers and units exactly; check w/v, w/w and v/v.
3. Check the scale of the master formula before calculating.

## Viva questions

1. **What is a pharmacopoeia?** A legally recognised book of drug standards published under government authority.
2. **Who publishes the IP?** The Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad.
3. **What are general notices?** Rules and meanings of terms that apply to the whole pharmacopoeia.
4. **What is a master formula?** The official formula of a preparation for a stated quantity.
5. **What is a working formula?** The master formula scaled to the quantity to be prepared.
6. **Is Martindale an official book of standards?** No, it is a reference book of drug information.

# Simple Syrup IP

**Aim:** To prepare and dispense 100 g of Simple Syrup.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ.

## Principle

Simple Syrup is a concentrated solution of **sucrose in purified water (66.7% w/w)**. At this concentration there is so little free water that microorganisms cannot grow, so it is **self-preserving**. Gentle heat speeds dissolution, but too much heat causes **inversion** of sucrose (into glucose and fructose) and darkening (caramelisation).

## Formula

| Ingredient | Master formula | Quantity for 100 g |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sucrose | 66.7 g | 66.7 g |
| Purified water | to 100 g | to 100 g |

## Requirements

Sucrose, purified water, beaker, glass rod, water bath, balance, muslin cloth, amber or clear glass bottle.

## Procedure

1. Weigh the beaker (tare) and weigh 66.7 g of sucrose into it.
2. Add about 33 ml of purified water.
3. Heat on a water bath with stirring until the sugar dissolves completely; do not boil.
4. Strain through muslin while hot.
5. Cool, then add purified water to make the total weight **100 g**.
6. Mix well and transfer to a clean, dry bottle; close tightly.

## Observations

Clear, colourless, viscous, sweet liquid.

## Result

100 g of Simple Syrup IP was prepared and dispensed.

## Label

Simple Syrup IP, 100 g. Store in a cool place in a well-closed container.

## Precautions

1. Do not overheat (inversion and caramelisation).
2. Make up to weight, not volume, because the formula is w/w.
3. Use clean dry bottles; avoid sugar crystals on the neck (cap locking).

## Viva questions

1. **What is the concentration of Simple Syrup IP?** 66.7% w/w sucrose (USP: 85% w/v).
2. **Why is it self-preserving?** High osmotic pressure; little free water for microbes.
3. **What is inversion?** Hydrolysis of sucrose into glucose and fructose by heat and acid.
4. **Uses of simple syrup?** Sweetening agent and vehicle; base for medicated syrups; binder in tablet granulation.

# Piperazine Citrate Elixir

**Aim:** To prepare and dispense 50 ml of Piperazine Citrate Elixir.

> The formula below is a typical official-type formula used in D.Pharm laboratories. Use the formula and flavour given in your lab manual where they differ.

## Principle

An **elixir** is a clear, sweetened, flavoured liquid for oral use. Piperazine citrate is freely soluble in water; glycerin and syrup sweeten it and add body. It is an **anthelmintic** used against roundworm and threadworm.

## Formula

| --- | --- | --- |
| Piperazine citrate | 18.75 g | 9.375 g |
| Glycerin | 5 ml | 2.5 ml |
| Syrup | 62.5 ml | 31.25 ml |
| Flavour (lemon/orange) and colour | q.s. | q.s. |
| Purified water | to 100 ml | to 50 ml |

## Requirements

Piperazine citrate, glycerin, syrup, flavour, purified water, beaker, measuring cylinder, glass rod, filter paper, funnel, amber bottle.

## Procedure

1. Weigh the piperazine citrate and dissolve it in about 10 ml of purified water.
2. Add the glycerin and syrup and mix well.
3. Add flavour (and colour if used) and stir.
4. Make up the volume to 50 ml with purified water.
5. Filter if not clear and transfer to a clean bottle.

## Observations

Clear, sweet, flavoured liquid.

## Result

50 ml of Piperazine Citrate Elixir was prepared and dispensed.

## Label

Piperazine Citrate Elixir, 50 ml. Dose: as directed by the physician. Store in a cool place.

## Precautions

1. Weigh the drug accurately (potent anthelmintic).
2. Dissolve the drug completely before adding syrup.
3. Use a clean amber bottle.

## Viva questions

1. **What is an elixir?** A clear, sweetened, flavoured hydroalcoholic or aqueous liquid for oral use.
2. **Use of piperazine?** Anthelmintic for roundworm and threadworm.
3. **Role of glycerin?** Sweetener, solvent and adds viscosity.
4. **Difference between syrup and elixir?** Syrup is a concentrated sugar solution; elixir is less sweet, clear and usually contains alcohol.

# Aqueous Iodine Solution (Lugol's Solution)

**Aim:** To prepare and dispense 50 ml of Aqueous Iodine Solution.

## Principle

Iodine is only very slightly soluble in water, but dissolves readily in a concentrated solution of potassium iodide because it forms the soluble **tri-iodide ion** (complexation):

```text
I2 + KI → KI3 (soluble)
```

So potassium iodide is first dissolved in a **small** amount of water, and the iodine is dissolved in this concentrated solution before dilution.

## Formula

| Ingredient | For 100 ml | For 50 ml |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Iodine | 5 g | 2.5 g |
| Potassium iodide | 10 g | 5 g |
| Purified water | to 100 ml | to 50 ml |

## Requirements

Iodine, potassium iodide, purified water, glass-stoppered weighing bottle, beaker, measuring cylinder, glass rod, amber glass-stoppered bottle.

## Procedure

1. Weigh 5 g of potassium iodide and dissolve it in about 5 ml of purified water.
2. Weigh 2.5 g of iodine in a glass weighing bottle (iodine attacks metal pans and paper).
3. Add the iodine to the concentrated KI solution and stir until completely dissolved.
4. Make up to 50 ml with purified water and mix.
5. Transfer to an amber bottle with a glass stopper.

## Observations

Deep brown, clear solution with the smell of iodine.

## Result

50 ml of Aqueous Iodine Solution was prepared and dispensed.

## Label

Aqueous Iodine Solution, 50 ml. Store in a cool place, protected from light, in a glass-stoppered bottle.

## Precautions

1. Dissolve KI in minimum water first, otherwise iodine will not dissolve.
2. Do not weigh iodine on paper or metal; use glass.
3. Avoid rubber or cork closures (iodine attacks them).

## Viva questions

1. **Why is KI added?** It forms soluble KI3 with iodine (complexation).
2. **Uses?** Iodine supplement, before thyroid surgery to reduce gland vascularity, in thyrotoxicosis.
3. **Why amber bottle?** To protect from light.
4. **Other name?** Lugol's solution.
practicals.title: Aqueous Iodine Solution (Lugol's solution)

# Castor Oil Emulsion

**Aim:** To prepare and dispense 100 ml of Castor Oil Emulsion by the dry gum method.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual where it differs.

## Principle

Castor oil is a **fixed oil**. With acacia as the emulsifying agent it forms an **oil-in-water** emulsion. In the dry gum method, the primary emulsion is made in the ratio **oil : water : gum = 4 : 2 : 1** for fixed oils. Acacia forms a protective film around each oil globule and prevents them from joining. Castor oil is a **stimulant laxative**; the emulsion masks its unpleasant taste and oiliness.

## Formula

| Ingredient | Quantity for 100 ml |
| --- | --- |
| Castor oil | 40 ml |
| Acacia (powdered) | 10 g |
| Purified water (for primary emulsion) | 20 ml |
| Syrup | 10 ml |
| Flavour (e.g. peppermint or cinnamon water) | q.s. |
| Purified water | to 100 ml |

## Requirements

Castor oil, acacia, syrup, flavour, purified water, dry porcelain mortar and pestle, measuring cylinders, bottle.

## Procedure

1. Measure 40 ml castor oil into a **dry** mortar.
2. Add 10 g acacia and triturate lightly just to disperse it (do not over-mix).
3. Add all 20 ml of water **at once** and triturate rapidly in one direction until a thick, white primary emulsion forms with a **clicking (crackling) sound**.
4. Add more water slowly with trituration to dilute.
5. Add syrup and flavour and mix.
6. Transfer to a measuring cylinder, rinse the mortar with water, and make up to 100 ml.
7. Transfer to a bottle and shake.

## Observations

Thick, white, creamy liquid. **Dilution test:** a drop mixes readily with water → o/w emulsion.

## Result

100 ml of Castor Oil Emulsion (o/w) was prepared and dispensed.

## Label

Castor Oil Emulsion, 100 ml. Shake well before use. Store in a cool place.

## Precautions

1. Mortar, pestle and measuring cylinder for oil must be dry.
2. Add the water for the primary emulsion all at once.
3. Triturate quickly in one direction until the click is heard.

## Viva questions

1. **Ratio for a fixed oil?** 4 : 2 : 1 (oil : water : gum).
2. **Type of emulsion?** Oil-in-water.
3. **Why is the mortar dry?** Water would wet the gum first and form lumps.
4. **Wet gum method?** Gum is made into mucilage with water first, then oil is added gradually.
5. **Use of castor oil?** Stimulant laxative.
practicals.title: Castor Oil Emulsion

# Cod Liver Oil Emulsion

**Aim:** To prepare and dispense 100 ml of Cod Liver Oil Emulsion.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual where it differs.

## Principle

Cod liver oil is a **fixed oil** rich in **vitamins A and D**. It is emulsified with acacia (primary emulsion **4 : 2 : 1**) to make an **o/w emulsion**, which masks the fishy taste and odour and is easier to take. A sweetener and flavour improve palatability. Vitamins A and D are sensitive to light and air, so the product is stored in a well-filled amber bottle.

## Formula

| Ingredient | Quantity for 100 ml |
| --- | --- |
| Cod liver oil | 40 ml |
| Acacia | 10 g |
| Purified water (primary emulsion) | 20 ml |
| Syrup | 10 ml |
| Flavour (e.g. cinnamon or peppermint) | q.s. |
| Preservative (as per manual) | q.s. |
| Purified water | to 100 ml |

## Requirements

Cod liver oil, acacia, syrup, flavour, preservative, purified water, dry mortar and pestle, measuring cylinders, amber bottle.

## Procedure

1. Place 40 ml cod liver oil in a dry mortar and add 10 g acacia; triturate briefly.
2. Add 20 ml water at once and triturate rapidly until a white, clicking primary emulsion forms.
3. Dilute gradually with water while triturating.
4. Add syrup, preservative and flavour.
5. Make up to 100 ml with water, transfer to an amber bottle and shake.

## Observations

White, creamy emulsion; dilutes easily with water (o/w). On standing it may cream; shaking redisperses it.

## Result

100 ml of Cod Liver Oil Emulsion was prepared and dispensed.

## Label

Cod Liver Oil Emulsion, 100 ml. Shake well before use. Store in a cool place, protected from light.

## Precautions

1. Use a dry mortar.
2. Do not delay adding the water for the primary emulsion.
3. Fill the bottle well and protect from light and air.

## Viva questions

1. **Vitamins present in cod liver oil?** Vitamins A and D.
2. **Why amber bottle?** Vitamins are light-sensitive and the oil can go rancid.
3. **Creaming or cracking – which is reversible?** Creaming.
4. **Test for type of emulsion?** Dilution, dye, conductivity tests.
practicals.title: Cod Liver Oil Emulsion

# Calamine Lotion

**Aim:** To prepare and dispense 100 ml of Calamine Lotion.

## Principle

Calamine lotion is a **suspension** of insoluble powders (calamine and zinc oxide) for external use. **Bentonite** is the suspending agent and **sodium citrate** acts as a **flocculating agent**, giving a loose sediment that is easy to redisperse. Glycerin helps the powder stick to the skin, and liquefied phenol is an antipruritic and preservative. The lotion is mildly astringent, soothing and cooling and is used for itching, sunburn and insect bites.

## Formula (BP type)

| Ingredient | Quantity for 100 ml |
| --- | --- |
| Calamine | 15 g |
| Zinc oxide | 5 g |
| Bentonite | 3 g |
| Sodium citrate | 0.5 g |
| Liquefied phenol | 0.5 ml |
| Glycerin | 5 ml |
| Purified water (freshly boiled and cooled) | to 100 ml |

## Requirements

All ingredients, mortar and pestle, sieve, measuring cylinder, bottle.

## Procedure

1. Weigh calamine, zinc oxide and bentonite, sieve them and mix in a mortar.
2. Dissolve sodium citrate in about 70 ml of water.
3. Triturate the mixed powders with the glycerin and a little of the citrate solution to a smooth paste.
4. Add the rest of the citrate solution gradually with trituration.
5. Add the liquefied phenol and mix.
6. Transfer to a measuring cylinder and make up to 100 ml; pour into a bottle.

## Observations

Pink, smooth suspension. On standing a loose sediment forms which redisperses on gentle shaking.

## Result

100 ml of Calamine Lotion was prepared and dispensed.

## Label

Calamine Lotion, 100 ml. **For external use only. Shake well before use.** Apply to the affected area.

## Precautions

1. Sieve powders to remove grit.
2. Make a smooth paste before diluting.
3. Handle phenol carefully (caustic).

## Viva questions

1. **What is calamine?** Zinc carbonate (or zinc oxide) coloured pink with a little ferric oxide.
2. **Role of bentonite?** Suspending agent.
3. **Role of sodium citrate?** Flocculating agent; gives loose, easily redispersed sediment.
4. **Role of glycerin?** Helps adhesion to the skin and wetting of powders.
5. **Lotion vs liniment?** Lotion is applied without friction; liniment with rubbing.
practicals.title: Calamine Lotion

# Magnesium Hydroxide Mixture

**Aim:** To prepare and dispense 100 ml of Magnesium Hydroxide Mixture.

> The formula below follows the older BP method by double decomposition. Use the preservative and quantities given in your lab manual.

## Principle

Magnesium hydroxide is an insoluble antacid and laxative. It is prepared freshly by **double decomposition** of magnesium sulphate with sodium hydroxide, which gives a very fine, gelatinous precipitate that stays well suspended:

```text
MgSO4 + 2 NaOH → Mg(OH)2 ↓ + Na2SO4
```

The by-product sodium sulphate is removed by washing. Light magnesium oxide is added; it slowly hydrates to more magnesium hydroxide (MgO + H2O → Mg(OH)2).

## Formula

| Ingredient | For 1000 ml (master) | For 100 ml (working) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Magnesium sulphate | 47.5 g | 4.75 g |
| Sodium hydroxide | 15 g | 1.5 g |
| Light magnesium oxide | 52.5 g | 5.25 g |
| Preservative | q.s. | q.s. |
| Purified water | to 1000 ml | to 100 ml |

## Requirements

Magnesium sulphate, sodium hydroxide, light magnesium oxide, purified water, beakers, glass rod, filter/strainer (muslin), measuring cylinder, bottle.

## Procedure

1. Dissolve magnesium sulphate in about 30 ml of water.
2. Dissolve sodium hydroxide in about 30 ml of water (in a separate beaker; this gets warm).
3. Add the magnesium sulphate solution slowly to the sodium hydroxide solution with constant stirring. A white gelatinous precipitate forms.
4. Allow to settle, decant the clear liquid and wash the precipitate with water several times (or on muslin) to remove sodium sulphate.
5. Mix the light magnesium oxide with a little water to a smooth cream and add to the washed precipitate.
6. Add preservative, make up to 100 ml with water and mix well.

## Observations

White, opaque, smooth suspension.

## Result

100 ml of Magnesium Hydroxide Mixture was prepared and dispensed.

## Label

Magnesium Hydroxide Mixture, 100 ml. **Shake well before use.** Store in a cool place; do not freeze.

## Precautions

1. Add magnesium sulphate solution to the alkali slowly with stirring for a fine precipitate.
2. Wash the precipitate well to remove sodium sulphate.
3. Handle sodium hydroxide with care.

## Viva questions

1. **Method of preparation?** Double decomposition (chemical reaction).
2. **Uses?** Antacid (small dose) and saline laxative (larger dose).
3. **Why is sodium sulphate removed?** It is an unwanted by-product with laxative action and affects taste.
4. **Why shake before use?** It is a suspension.
practicals.title: Magnesium Hydroxide Mixture

# Simple Ointment base and Sulphur Ointment

**Aim:** (a) To prepare 50 g of Simple Ointment (base) by fusion. (b) To prepare 20 g of Sulphur Ointment by incorporation (trituration).

## Principle

**Simple Ointment** is an oleaginous/absorption base. It is made by the **fusion method**: ingredients are melted together, starting with the one of highest melting point, and stirred until cool so the product is smooth. Wool fat helps the base take up some water; cetostearyl alcohol makes it stiffer and helps emulsify.

**Sulphur Ointment** contains 10% precipitated sulphur in Simple Ointment. Sulphur is insoluble, so it is incorporated by **levigation (trituration)** on an ointment slab. It is used for scabies, acne and fungal skin infections (keratolytic and parasiticide).

## Formula

**(a) Simple Ointment**

| Ingredient | For 100 g (master) | For 50 g |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wool fat | 5 g | 2.5 g |
| Hard paraffin | 5 g | 2.5 g |
| Cetostearyl alcohol | 5 g | 2.5 g |
| White (or yellow) soft paraffin | 85 g | 42.5 g |

**(b) Sulphur Ointment**

| Ingredient | For 100 g | For 20 g |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Precipitated sulphur (finely sifted) | 10 g | 2 g |
| Simple Ointment | 90 g | 18 g |

## Requirements

Ingredients, evaporating dish, water bath, glass rod, ointment slab, spatula, sieve, ointment jars.

## Procedure

**(a) Simple Ointment**

1. Weigh all ingredients.
2. Melt hard paraffin and cetostearyl alcohol together on a water bath.
3. Add wool fat and soft paraffin and melt.
4. Remove from the bath and stir continuously until the base cools and sets.
5. Fill into a jar.

**(b) Sulphur Ointment**

1. Sift the sulphur through a fine sieve.
2. Place sulphur on the ointment slab and levigate with a small amount of Simple Ointment using a spatula to make a smooth paste.
3. Add the rest of the base in portions (geometric dilution) and mix until uniform.
4. Fill into a jar, smooth the surface and close.

## Observations

Simple Ointment: smooth, white/yellowish, greasy semisolid. Sulphur Ointment: uniform pale yellow ointment, free from grit.

## Result

50 g of Simple Ointment and 20 g of Sulphur Ointment were prepared and dispensed.

## Label

Sulphur Ointment, 20 g. **For external use only.** Apply as directed.

## Precautions

1. Melt in decreasing order of melting point; avoid overheating.
2. Stir until set, otherwise the ointment becomes granular.
3. Sift the sulphur and levigate well so there are no gritty particles.

## Viva questions

1. **Method for simple ointment?** Fusion.
2. **Method for sulphur ointment?** Trituration/incorporation (levigation).
3. **Uses of sulphur ointment?** Scabies, acne, fungal infections.
4. **Classes of ointment bases?** Oleaginous, absorption, emulsion (w/o, o/w), water-soluble.
5. **Why stir till cool?** To get a smooth, uniform product.
practicals.title: Simple Ointment base and Sulphur Ointment

# Cetrimide Cream

**Aim:** To prepare and dispense 50 g of Cetrimide Cream.

## Principle

Cetrimide is a **cationic surfactant** with antiseptic action. In this cream it also acts with **cetostearyl alcohol** as an emulsifying system, giving an **oil-in-water** cream that is non-greasy and water-washable. The oil phase (cetostearyl alcohol and liquid paraffin) and the water phase are heated separately to the same temperature, mixed, and stirred until cool. Used as an antiseptic for cuts, burns and minor skin infections.

## Formula (BPC type)

| Ingredient | For 100 g | For 50 g |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cetrimide | 0.5 g | 0.25 g |
| Cetostearyl alcohol | 5 g | 2.5 g |
| Liquid paraffin | 50 g | 25 g |
| Purified water (freshly boiled and cooled) | to 100 g | to 50 g |

## Requirements

Ingredients, two beakers, water bath, thermometer, glass rod or stirrer, ointment jar.

## Procedure

1. Melt the cetostearyl alcohol with the liquid paraffin on a water bath and keep at about 60–70 °C.
2. Dissolve the cetrimide in the water and heat to the same temperature.
3. Add the aqueous phase to the oily phase gradually with continuous stirring.
4. Remove from heat and stir until the cream cools and thickens.
5. Adjust to 50 g with water if needed, mix and fill into a jar.

## Observations

White, smooth, non-greasy cream; mixes with water (o/w).

## Result

50 g of Cetrimide Cream was prepared and dispensed.

## Label

Cetrimide Cream, 50 g. **For external use only.** Store in a cool place.

## Precautions

1. Both phases must be at the same temperature before mixing.
2. Stir continuously until cool.
3. Do not mix with soaps or anionic substances (they inactivate cetrimide).

## Viva questions

1. **Type of cream?** Oil-in-water (vanishing type).
2. **Nature of cetrimide?** Cationic quaternary ammonium compound; antiseptic.
3. **Incompatible with?** Soaps and anionic surfactants.
4. **Difference between cream and ointment?** Cream is an emulsion, softer and less greasy.
practicals.title: Cetrimide Cream

# Sodium Alginate Gel

**Aim:** To prepare and dispense 50 g of Sodium Alginate Gel.

> Gel strength depends on the grade of sodium alginate. Use the concentration given in your lab manual; the formula below is typical.

## Principle

Sodium alginate is a natural polysaccharide (from brown seaweeds). In water it hydrates and swells to form a viscous **gel**. Glycerin wets the powder (preventing lumps) and acts as a humectant; a preservative such as methylparaben prevents microbial growth. Alginate gels are used as lubricants and as bases for topical drugs.

## Formula

| Ingredient | For 100 g | For 50 g |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sodium alginate | 5 g | 2.5 g |
| Glycerin | 10 g | 5 g |
| Methylparaben | 0.2 g | 0.1 g |
| Purified water | to 100 g | to 50 g |

## Requirements

Ingredients, mortar and pestle or beaker with stirrer, water bath, ointment jar or collapsible tube.

## Procedure

1. Dissolve methylparaben in hot purified water and cool.
2. Triturate sodium alginate with glycerin in a mortar to a smooth slurry (this stops lumping).
3. Add the water gradually with continuous trituration.
4. Allow to stand so the gum hydrates fully and air bubbles escape.
5. Make up to weight with water, mix and fill into a jar or tube.

## Observations

Clear to slightly opalescent, smooth, viscous gel.

## Result

50 g of Sodium Alginate Gel was prepared and dispensed.

## Label

Sodium Alginate Gel, 50 g. For external use. Store in a cool place.

## Precautions

1. Wet the alginate with glycerin first, else lumps (fish eyes) form.
2. Avoid calcium salts unless intended; they make alginate set into a firm gel.
3. Allow complete hydration before final weighing.

## Viva questions

1. **Source of alginate?** Brown seaweeds (alginic acid salts).
2. **Role of glycerin?** Dispersing/wetting agent and humectant.
3. **Other gelling agents?** Carbomer, tragacanth, methylcellulose, sodium CMC, gelatin.
4. **Advantages of gels?** Non-greasy, cooling, easily washed off.
practicals.title: Sodium Alginate Gel

practicals.markdown:
# Turpentine Liniment and White Liniment

**Aim:** To prepare and dispense (a) 50 ml of Turpentine Liniment and (b) 50 ml of White Liniment.

## Principle

Liniments are liquid preparations rubbed into the skin with friction. Both these liniments are **emulsions** containing **turpentine oil**, a counter-irritant and rubefacient used for muscle pain, sprains and stiffness.

- **Turpentine Liniment:** soft soap (potassium soap) is the emulsifying agent; camphor adds counter-irritant action.
- **White Liniment:** oleic acid reacts with ammonia to form **ammonium oleate** soap **in situ**, which emulsifies the turpentine oil; ammonium chloride helps give a creamy, stable product.

## Formula

**(a) Turpentine Liniment**

| Ingredient | For 1000 ml (master) | For 50 ml |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Camphor | 50 g | 2.5 g |
| Soft soap | 75 g | 3.75 g |
| Turpentine oil | 650 ml | 32.5 ml |
| Purified water | 225 ml | 11.25 ml |

**(b) White Liniment**

| Ingredient | For 1000 ml (master) | For 50 ml |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ammonium chloride | 12.5 g | 0.625 g |
| Dilute ammonia solution | 45 ml | 2.25 ml |
| Oleic acid | 85 ml | 4.25 ml |
| Turpentine oil | 250 ml | 12.5 ml |
| Purified water | 625 ml | 31.25 ml |

## Requirements

Ingredients, mortar and pestle, measuring cylinders, bottles (coloured, fluted if available).

## Procedure

**(a) Turpentine Liniment**

1. Dissolve camphor in the turpentine oil.
2. Triturate the soft soap with the water in a mortar to a smooth liquid.
3. Add the camphor–turpentine solution in small portions with vigorous trituration (or shaking in a bottle) until a creamy emulsion forms.
4. Transfer to a bottle.

**(b) White Liniment**

1. Mix the oleic acid with the turpentine oil in a bottle.
2. Dissolve the ammonium chloride in the water and add the dilute ammonia solution.
3. Add this aqueous solution to the oily mixture and shake vigorously until a white creamy emulsion forms.

## Observations

Both form white, creamy emulsions with a turpentine smell.

## Result

50 ml each of Turpentine Liniment and White Liniment were prepared and dispensed.

## Label

**For external use only. Not to be applied to broken or inflamed skin. Shake well before use.** Rub into the affected part. Flammable – keep away from flame.

## Precautions

1. Turpentine oil is flammable and irritant – no open flames.
2. Add the oil phase gradually with vigorous mixing.
3. Use a coloured, fluted (poison-type) bottle as per lab practice.

## Viva questions

1. **What is a liniment?** Liquid or semi-liquid preparation applied with friction.
2. **Emulsifier in white liniment?** Ammonium oleate formed in situ from oleic acid and ammonia.
3. **Emulsifier in turpentine liniment?** Soft soap.
4. **Action of turpentine oil?** Counter-irritant and rubefacient.
5. **Why not on broken skin?** Causes irritation and absorption of irritants.
practicals.title: Turpentine Liniment and White Liniment

# Effervescent granules

**Aim:** To prepare and dispense 50 g of effervescent granules by the fusion (heat) method.

> Many manuals use a named product such as effervescent sodium citrotartrate or effervescent potassium citrate granules. Follow the drug and quantities in your manual; the calculation below shows how the acid and base are balanced.

## Principle

Citric acid and tartaric acid react with sodium bicarbonate in water to release **carbon dioxide**, making a fizzy, pleasant drink:

```text
C6H8O7·H2O (citric acid, 210) + 3 NaHCO3 (3 × 84) → Na3C6H5O7 + 3 CO2 + 4 H2O
C4H6O6 (tartaric acid, 150)   + 2 NaHCO3 (2 × 84) → Na2C4H4O6 + 2 CO2 + 2 H2O
```

Citric acid alone gives a sticky mass, tartaric acid alone gives crumbly granules, so they are used together in the ratio **citric : tartaric = 1 : 2**. In the **fusion method**, gentle heat releases the **water of crystallisation of citric acid**, which moistens the powder and acts as the binder.

## Calculation of sodium bicarbonate

```text
1 g citric acid   needs 252 ÷ 210 = 1.2 g NaHCO3
1 g tartaric acid needs 168 ÷ 150 = 1.12 g NaHCO3
For 1 g citric + 2 g tartaric: 1.2 + 2.24 = 3.44 g NaHCO3
So citric acid : tartaric acid : sodium bicarbonate = 1 : 2 : 3.44
```

## Typical formula (for about 50 g)

| Ingredient | Quantity |
| --- | --- |
| Citric acid (monohydrate) | 5 g |
| Tartaric acid | 10 g |
| Sodium bicarbonate | 17.2 g |
| Drug (as per manual) | as directed |
| Sucrose (powdered) | to 50 g |

## Requirements

Ingredients, mortar and pestle, sieves (about no. 10 and no. 20), evaporating dish or tray, oven or water bath, thermometer, airtight bottle.

## Procedure

1. Dry all ingredients and powder them separately; pass through a sieve.
2. Mix the citric acid and tartaric acid with the sucrose and drug, then add the sodium bicarbonate and mix lightly.
3. Spread the powder on a dish and heat in an oven (about 93–104 °C) or on a water bath, turning with a spatula, until the mass becomes damp and coherent.
4. Quickly pass the damp mass through a coarse sieve to form granules.
5. Dry the granules at not more than about 50 °C.
6. Pass through a finer sieve to remove fines and pack at once in an airtight bottle.

## Observations

White, dry granules that effervesce briskly when added to water.

## Result

50 g of effervescent granules were prepared and dispensed.

## Label

Effervescent granules, 50 g. **Dissolve the dose in water and drink during effervescence.** Keep the container tightly closed in a dry place.

## Precautions

1. Use dry ingredients and dry apparatus; moisture starts the reaction early.
2. Do not overheat; work quickly once the mass is damp.
3. Pack immediately in airtight containers.

## Viva questions

1. **Why use both citric and tartaric acid?** Citric acid alone is sticky; tartaric alone gives friable granules.
2. **What acts as binder in the fusion method?** Water of crystallisation of citric acid.
3. **Gas released?** Carbon dioxide.
4. **Why granules rather than powder?** Less hygroscopic, controlled effervescence, better flow.
practicals.title: Effervescent granules

practicals.markdown:
# Dusting powder (Zinc, Starch and Talc)

**Aim:** To prepare and dispense 50 g of Zinc, Starch and Talc Dusting Powder.

## Principle

Dusting powders are fine, free-flowing powders applied to the skin. **Zinc oxide** is mildly astringent and antiseptic, **starch** is absorbent and soothing, and **talc** is a lubricant that helps the powder spread. Powders are mixed by **geometric (doubling-up) dilution** and passed through a fine sieve so they are smooth and free from grit. Powders meant for wounds or broken skin must be sterile, because talc and starch may contain bacterial spores.

## Formula

| Ingredient | For 100 g | For 50 g |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zinc oxide | 25 g | 12.5 g |
| Starch | 25 g | 12.5 g |
| Purified talc | 50 g | 25 g |

## Requirements

Ingredients, mortar and pestle, fine sieve (e.g. sieve no. 120), spatula, sifter-top container.

## Procedure

1. Weigh all ingredients and sieve each separately.
2. Place zinc oxide in the mortar, add an equal amount of starch and triturate.
3. Add the rest of the starch, then the talc, in portions equal to the mixture already present, triturating after each addition.
4. Pass the whole mixture through the fine sieve and mix again lightly.
5. Fill into a sifter-top container.

## Observations

White, smooth, fine, free-flowing powder without grit.

## Result

50 g of Zinc, Starch and Talc Dusting Powder was prepared and dispensed.

## Label

Dusting Powder, 50 g. **For external use only. Not to be applied to open wounds or broken skin.** Store in a dry place.

## Precautions

1. Sieve to remove grit.
2. Use geometric dilution for uniform mixing.
3. Keep dry; sterilise if meant for wounds.

## Viva questions

1. **What is a dusting powder?** A fine powder applied to the skin for local action.
2. **Why must dusting powders for wounds be sterile?** Talc may carry spores of bacteria such as tetanus.
3. **Role of talc?** Lubricant, helps spreading.
4. **What is an insufflation?** A powder blown into a body cavity with an insufflator.

# Sodium Chloride Injection (Normal Saline, 0.9% w/v)

**Aim:** To prepare and dispense 100 ml of Sodium Chloride Injection IP (0.9% w/v).

## Principle

A **0.9% w/v** solution of sodium chloride is **isotonic** with blood (freezing point about −0.52 °C). It is used to replace fluid and electrolytes, as a vehicle for other injections, and to flush IV lines. Every injection must be **sterile, pyrogen-free, clear (free from particles)** and isotonic. It is prepared in **Water for Injections**, filtered, filled into clean containers, sealed and sterilised by **autoclaving at 121 °C for 15 minutes**.

## Formula

| Ingredient | Quantity |
| --- | --- |
| Sodium chloride (injection grade) | 0.9 g |
| Water for Injections | to 100 ml |

## Requirements

Sodium chloride, Water for Injections, beaker, volumetric flask, sintered glass or membrane filter assembly, clean glass vials/ampoules or infusion bottle with closures, autoclave.

## Procedure

1. Wash containers with detergent, rinse with purified water and finally with Water for Injections; sterilise/dry as directed.
2. Weigh 0.9 g sodium chloride and dissolve in about 80 ml Water for Injections.
3. Make up to 100 ml in a volumetric flask.
4. Filter through a clean sintered glass or membrane filter until perfectly clear.
5. Fill into the containers (a slight excess over labelled volume), seal ampoules or close and crimp vials/bottles.
6. Sterilise in an autoclave at **121 °C for 15 minutes**.
7. Inspect for clarity against black and white backgrounds and do a leakage test for ampoules.

## Observations

Clear, colourless solution, free from visible particles.

## Result

100 ml of Sodium Chloride Injection (0.9% w/v) was prepared, sterilised and dispensed.

## Label

Sodium Chloride Injection IP 0.9% w/v, 100 ml. Sterile. For intravenous use. Batch number, date of manufacture and expiry. Discard any unused portion.

## Precautions

1. Use injection-grade materials and Water for Injections only.
2. Work in a clean area; avoid particles and fibres.
3. Check autoclave temperature and time.

## Viva questions

1. **Why 0.9%?** It is isotonic with blood.
2. **What is Water for Injections?** Pyrogen-free water prepared by distillation (or equivalent process), meant for making injections.
3. **Sterilisation used?** Autoclaving at 121 °C for 15 minutes.
4. **What are pyrogens?** Fever-producing substances, mainly bacterial endotoxins.
5. **Leakage test?** Ampoules placed in a dye solution under vacuum; leaking ones become coloured.
practicals.title: Sodium Chloride Injection (normal saline)

# Calcium Gluconate Injection (10% w/v)

**Aim:** To prepare and dispense Calcium Gluconate Injection 10% w/v (for example 5 ampoules of 10 ml).

> Follow the stabiliser quantity and container type given in your lab manual.

## Principle

Calcium gluconate is soluble only to a limited extent in cold water, so a 10% solution is **supersaturated** and is made by dissolving the salt in **hot** Water for Injections. A small amount of **calcium saccharate** is added as a **stabiliser** to stop calcium gluconate crystallising out on storage. The solution is filtered, filled into ampoules and **sterilised by autoclaving**. It is used in hypocalcaemia (tetany) and some cases of hyperkalaemia.

## Formula

| Ingredient | For 100 ml |
| --- | --- |
| Calcium gluconate | 10 g |
| Calcium saccharate (stabiliser) | small quantity, as per manual |
| Water for Injections | to 100 ml |

## Requirements

Calcium gluconate, calcium saccharate, Water for Injections, beaker, water bath, volumetric flask, sintered glass/membrane filter, ampoules, ampoule sealing burner, autoclave.

## Procedure

1. Clean ampoules: wash, rinse with Water for Injections and dry/sterilise.
2. Heat about 80 ml Water for Injections to near boiling.
3. Dissolve the calcium saccharate and then the calcium gluconate in the hot water with stirring.
4. Cool, make up to 100 ml with Water for Injections.
5. Filter until clear.
6. Fill 10 ml (plus a slight excess) into each ampoule and seal by fusion.
7. Sterilise by autoclaving at 121 °C for 15 minutes.
8. Inspect for clarity and perform the leakage test.

## Observations

Clear, colourless solution free from crystals and particles.

## Result

Calcium Gluconate Injection 10% w/v was prepared, sterilised and dispensed.

## Label

Calcium Gluconate Injection IP 10% w/v, 10 ml ampoule. Sterile. For slow intravenous injection. Batch number, manufacturing and expiry dates.

## Precautions

1. Dissolve in hot water; do not let the solution crystallise before filtering.
2. Inspect for crystals after sterilisation and on storage.
3. Seal ampoules properly; check for leaks.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is calcium saccharate added?** As a stabiliser to prevent crystallisation of the supersaturated solution.
2. **Uses?** Hypocalcaemia and tetany; to protect the heart in hyperkalaemia.
3. **Route?** Slow intravenous injection.
4. **Why must injections be particle-free?** Particles can block small blood vessels and cause harm.
practicals.title: Calcium Gluconate Injection

# Tetracycline Capsules (hard gelatin)

**Aim:** To fill and dispense 10 hard gelatin capsules each containing 250 mg of tetracycline hydrochloride.

## Principle

Hard gelatin capsules are filled with powder by the **punch (hand-filling) method** or with a **capsule filling board**. A diluent is added if needed to fill the capsule body completely so that every capsule has the same volume of powder. **Calcium-containing diluents (such as dicalcium phosphate) must not be used** because calcium forms a complex with tetracycline and reduces its absorption; lactose is suitable. A small amount of lubricant helps flow.

## Formula (for 10 capsules, with one extra for loss)

| Ingredient | Per capsule | For 11 capsules |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tetracycline hydrochloride | 250 mg | 2.75 g |
| Lactose (diluent) | as needed to fill the shell | q.s. |
| Magnesium stearate | about 1% of fill | q.s. |

**Selecting the capsule size:** fill one empty shell of the chosen size (usually size 1 or 0) with the drug powder, weigh, and calculate the diluent needed to make the fill weight equal for all capsules.

## Requirements

Tetracycline hydrochloride, lactose, magnesium stearate, empty hard gelatin capsules, mortar and pestle, spatula, glass slab or capsule filling board, balance, gloves, airtight amber container.

## Procedure

1. Weigh the drug and diluent; mix by geometric dilution in a mortar; add lubricant and mix lightly.
2. Spread the powder on a clean slab to a uniform depth of about half the body length.
3. Hold the capsule body and press (punch) it repeatedly into the powder until filled; fit the cap. (With a filling board: place bodies in the holes, spread powder over, level with a spatula, then replace caps.)
4. Weigh each filled capsule and adjust to the calculated weight.
5. Wipe the capsules with a clean cloth to remove adhering powder.
6. Pack in a clean, dry, airtight container.

## Observations

| Capsule | Weight (mg) |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | |
| 2 | |
| … | |

Average weight = ___ mg; all within ±10% (fill below 300 mg) or ±7.5% (300 mg or more).

## Result

10 capsules of tetracycline hydrochloride 250 mg were filled and dispensed.

## Label

Tetracycline Capsules 250 mg, 10 capsules. Take as directed with water, not with milk or antacids. Complete the course. Store in a cool, dry place, protected from light.

## Precautions

1. Wear gloves; do not touch capsules with bare hands.
2. Avoid calcium salts as diluents.
3. Work in a dry atmosphere; shells soften in humidity and become brittle when too dry.

## Viva questions

1. **Why not take tetracycline with milk or antacids?** Calcium, magnesium and aluminium chelate tetracycline and reduce absorption.
2. **Largest and smallest capsule sizes?** 000 and 5.
3. **Composition of hard capsule shell?** Gelatin, water (13–16%), colour, opacifier.
4. **Disintegration time limit for capsules?** 30 minutes.
practicals.title: Tetracycline capsules (hard gelatin)

# Paracetamol Tablets (wet granulation)

**Aim:** To prepare paracetamol tablets (500 mg) by the wet granulation method and evaluate them.

> Batch size and excipient quantities are typical. Use the formula in your lab manual.

## Principle

Paracetamol powder flows and compresses poorly, so it is **granulated**. In wet granulation the drug and diluent/disintegrant are massed with a **binder solution** (starch paste), screened, dried, rescreened, lubricated and compressed. Starch acts as disintegrant; magnesium stearate and talc act as lubricant and glidant.

## Formula (for 50 tablets of 500 mg paracetamol)

| Ingredient | Per tablet | For 50 tablets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Paracetamol | 500 mg | 25 g |
| Starch (disintegrant, intragranular) | 40 mg | 2 g |
| Starch paste 10% (binder) | q.s. | q.s. |
| Starch (disintegrant, extragranular) | 20 mg | 1 g |
| Magnesium stearate | 5 mg | 0.25 g |
| Talc | 10 mg | 0.5 g |

## Requirements

Ingredients, mortar and pestle or planetary mixer, sieves (no. 10/12 and no. 16/20), tray dryer or oven, tablet machine (single punch), hardness tester, friabilator, disintegration apparatus.

## Procedure

1. **Starch paste:** disperse starch in cold water and heat with stirring until a translucent paste forms; cool.
2. **Dry mixing:** sieve paracetamol and starch; mix.
3. **Wet massing:** add starch paste gradually and knead until a damp mass forms that holds together when squeezed but crumbles when pressed (snow-ball test).
4. **Wet screening:** pass through sieve no. 10–12.
5. **Drying:** dry granules at about 50–60 °C until moisture is suitably low.
6. **Dry screening:** pass through sieve no. 16–20.
7. **Lubrication:** add the extragranular starch, talc and magnesium stearate (sieved) and mix gently.
8. **Compression:** set the die fill for the target weight and compress on a single punch machine.
9. Evaluate weight variation, hardness, friability and disintegration.

## Observations

| Test | Result | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Average weight | | ±5% (250 mg or more) |
| Hardness | | about 4–6 kg |
| Friability | | not more than 1% |
| Disintegration | | 15 minutes (uncoated) |

## Result

Paracetamol tablets 500 mg were prepared by wet granulation and evaluated.

## Label

Paracetamol Tablets IP 500 mg. Dose as directed; do not exceed the stated daily dose.

## Precautions

1. Do not over-wet the mass (hard granules) or under-wet it (fines, capping).
2. Dry granules properly to avoid sticking and picking.
3. Mix lubricants gently and briefly.

## Viva questions

1. **Why granulate?** To improve flow, compressibility and content uniformity.
2. **Role of starch?** Binder (as paste), disintegrant (dry), diluent.
3. **Causes of capping?** Air entrapment, too many fines, too dry granules.
4. **Friability limit?** Not more than 1% loss.
practicals.title: Paracetamol tablets (wet granulation)

# Common cosmetic preparations

**Aim:** To prepare at least five commonly used cosmetic preparations: cold cream, vanishing cream, shampoo, toothpaste and a hand/body lotion.

> Cosmetic formulas vary widely. The formulas below are typical laboratory formulas; use those in your manual where they differ. Each preparation is about 50 g or 50 ml.

## 1. Cold cream (w/o)

**Principle:** borax reacts with the free fatty acids (cerotic acid) of beeswax to form a **sodium soap** in situ, which emulsifies water in the oil phase, giving a **w/o** cream. Water evaporating from the skin gives a cooling feel.

| Ingredient | For 50 g |
| --- | --- |
| White beeswax | 8 g |
| Liquid paraffin | 25 g |
| Borax | 0.5 g |
| Purified water | 16.5 g |
| Perfume (rose) | q.s. |

**Procedure:** melt beeswax with liquid paraffin at about 70 °C. Dissolve borax in water heated to the same temperature. Add the borax solution slowly to the oil phase with stirring; stir until cool; add perfume below about 40 °C; fill into a jar.

## 2. Vanishing cream (o/w)

**Principle:** part of the **stearic acid** is neutralised by alkali to form a soap (potassium stearate), which emulsifies the rest of the stearic acid as an **o/w** cream. It spreads and "vanishes" leaving a thin non-greasy film.

| Ingredient | For 50 g |
| --- | --- |
| Stearic acid | 8 g |
| Potassium hydroxide | 0.5 g |
| Glycerin | 4 g |
| Purified water | to 50 g |
| Perfume, preservative | q.s. |

**Procedure:** melt stearic acid at about 70–75 °C. Dissolve KOH in water, add glycerin and heat to the same temperature. Add the aqueous phase to the melted acid with stirring; stir until cool and creamy; add perfume.

## 3. Shampoo (clear liquid)

| Ingredient | For 50 ml |
| --- | --- |
| Sodium lauryl ether sulphate (detergent) | 15 g |
| Coconut diethanolamide (foam booster, thickener) | 1.5 g |
| Sodium chloride (thickener) | about 0.5 g |
| Citric acid (to adjust pH about 5.5–6.5) | q.s. |
| Preservative, colour, perfume | q.s. |
| Purified water | to 50 ml |

**Procedure:** dissolve the detergent in most of the water with slow stirring (avoid foaming); add diethanolamide, preservative, colour and perfume; adjust pH; add salt slowly to thicken; make up to volume.

## 4. Toothpaste

| Ingredient | For 50 g | Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Calcium carbonate or dicalcium phosphate | 22 g | Abrasive (cleaning) |
| Glycerin or sorbitol | 12 g | Humectant (keeps paste moist) |
| Sodium carboxymethylcellulose | 0.6 g | Binder / thickener |
| Sodium lauryl sulphate | 0.75 g | Foaming agent, detergent |
| Saccharin sodium | 0.05 g | Sweetener |
| Peppermint oil | q.s. | Flavour |
| Preservative | q.s. | |
| Purified water | to 50 g | |

**Procedure:** disperse sodium CMC in glycerin, add water and allow to swell into a gel; add saccharin and preservative; add the abrasive in portions with thorough mixing; add SLS and flavour last with gentle mixing; fill into a tube.

## 5. Hand and body lotion (o/w)

| Ingredient | For 50 ml |
| --- | --- |
| Stearic acid | 1.5 g |
| Cetyl alcohol | 0.5 g |
| Liquid paraffin | 3 g |
| Triethanolamine | 0.5 g |
| Glycerin | 2.5 g |
| Preservative, perfume | q.s. |
| Purified water | to 50 ml |

**Procedure:** heat the oil phase (stearic acid, cetyl alcohol, liquid paraffin) and the aqueous phase (water, glycerin, triethanolamine) separately to about 70 °C; add aqueous to oil phase with stirring (triethanolamine stearate forms as emulsifier); stir until cool; add perfume.

## Result

Cold cream, vanishing cream, shampoo, toothpaste and hand lotion were prepared and packed.

## Precautions

1. Heat oil and water phases to the same temperature before mixing.
2. Add perfumes and volatile ingredients only after cooling.
3. Avoid air entrapment and excessive foaming.
4. Use clean, dry containers and add preservatives.

## Viva questions

1. **Emulsifier in cold cream?** Sodium soap formed from borax and free fatty acids of beeswax.
2. **Type of vanishing cream?** Oil-in-water.
3. **Role of humectant in toothpaste?** Keeps it moist and prevents hardening.
4. **Function of sodium lauryl sulphate?** Detergent and foaming agent.
5. **Why is shampoo pH kept slightly acidic?** To suit the scalp and hair and reduce irritation.
practicals.title: Common cosmetic preparations

# Demonstration of the stages of tablet manufacture

**Aim:** To study the stages of tablet manufacturing and the equipment used at each stage.

## Principle

A tablet is made by a chain of unit operations. In industry each stage is done with dedicated equipment under GMP, with in-process checks so that every tablet has the right weight, strength, hardness and appearance.

## Stages and equipment

```text
DISPENSING → SIFTING → DRY MIXING → WET GRANULATION → WET MILLING
   → DRYING → DRY MILLING / SIZING → LUBRICATION (BLENDING)
   → COMPRESSION → (COATING) → INSPECTION → PACKING
```

| Stage | Equipment | What to observe |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dispensing | Calibrated balances, dispensing booth with dust extraction | Weighing checked by a second person |
| Sifting | Vibratory sifter with mesh | Removal of lumps and foreign matter |
| Dry mixing / wet granulation | Rapid mixer granulator (impeller + chopper), planetary mixer | Binder added; end point of wet mass |
| Wet milling | Multi-mill or oscillating granulator | Uniform wet granules |
| Drying | Fluidized bed dryer or tray dryer | Loss on drying (moisture) checked |
| Dry milling / sizing | Multi-mill, sifter | Granule size distribution |
| Lubrication / blending | Double cone, octagonal or bin blender | Short blending time with lubricant |
| Compression | Rotary tablet press (die table, punches, cams, pressure rollers) | Weight, hardness, thickness, friability, disintegration checked at intervals |
| Coating | Coating pan or perforated pan, spray guns | Weight gain, appearance |
| Inspection | Inspection belt | Remove defective tablets (capping, chipping, spots) |
| Packing | Strip and blister packing machines | Seal integrity, batch printing |

## Procedure (demonstration)

1. Observe or watch each stage in the lab or on a demonstration model/video, or during the industrial visit.
2. Note the principle and main parts of each machine.
3. Note the in-process checks done at each stage.
4. Draw a flow chart and a labelled diagram of a rotary tablet press.

## Observations

Record the machines seen, their function and the in-process tests in a table like the one above.

## Result

The stages of tablet manufacture and the equipment and in-process controls used at each stage were studied.

## Precautions

1. Wear gloves, mask and cap in the processing area.
2. Do not touch moving machine parts.
3. Follow the instructions of the supervisor.

## Viva questions

1. **What is a rapid mixer granulator?** A mixer with an impeller and chopper used for dry mixing and wet granulation.
2. **How is drying end point checked?** By loss on drying (moisture content).
3. **Parts of a rotary press?** Hopper, feed frame, die table (turret), upper and lower punches, cams, pressure rollers.
4. **Why is lubricant blended briefly?** Over-mixing coats particles, softening tablets and slowing dissolution.
5. **What are in-process controls?** Checks during manufacture such as weight, hardness, thickness, friability and disintegration.
practicals.title: Stages of tablet manufacture (demonstration)

# Proper use and storage of dosage forms, inhalers, spacers and insulin pens

**Aim:** To learn and demonstrate the correct methods of using and storing common dosage forms, including special devices such as metered-dose inhalers, dry powder inhalers, spacers and insulin pens.

## Principle

A medicine works well only when it is used and stored correctly. Pharmacists must be able to show patients the right technique and explain storage, using placebo or demonstration devices.

## Requirements

Demonstration (placebo) metered-dose inhaler, dry powder inhaler, spacer, insulin pen with needles, empty strips, eye drop bottle, suppository model, patient information leaflets.

## Procedure / technique

**1. Metered-dose inhaler (MDI)**

1. Remove the cap and **shake** the inhaler well.
2. Breathe out fully, away from the mouthpiece.
3. Put the mouthpiece between the lips, seal them.
4. Start breathing in **slowly** and press the canister once at the same time.
5. Continue a slow, deep breath; **hold the breath for about 10 seconds**.
6. Wait about 30–60 seconds before a second puff.
7. After a steroid inhaler, **rinse the mouth** with water and spit (prevents oral thrush).

**2. MDI with spacer**

Fit the inhaler to the spacer, shake, press once into the spacer, then breathe in slowly and deeply (or take several normal breaths through the mouthpiece/mask). Useful for children, elderly and those who cannot coordinate pressing and breathing. Wash the spacer as directed and let it dry in air.

**3. Dry powder inhaler (DPI)**

Load the dose as per the device, breathe out away from the device (never into it), seal lips and breathe in **quickly and deeply**, hold the breath, then breathe out slowly. Keep the device dry.

**4. Insulin pen**

1. Wash hands; check the insulin type and expiry; roll cloudy insulin gently (do not shake hard).
2. Attach a new needle.
3. **Prime** by dialling 2 units and pressing with the pen upright, until a drop appears.
4. Dial the prescribed dose.
5. Pinch the skin (abdomen, thigh, upper arm), insert the needle (usually at 90°) and press the button fully.
6. **Hold for about 10 seconds** before withdrawing.
7. Remove and safely discard the needle; rotate injection sites.

**Storage of insulin:** unopened pens in a refrigerator at 2–8 °C, never frozen; the pen in use may be kept at room temperature away from heat and light for the period stated on the leaflet (often about 4 weeks).

**5. Other dosage forms (brief)**

| Dosage form | Correct use | Storage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tablets/capsules | Swallow with water; do not crush SR or enteric tablets | Cool, dry place, in original strip |
| Suspensions/emulsions | Shake well; use measuring cup or spoon | As labelled; reconstituted antibiotics in refrigerator, discard after stated days |
| Eye drops | Pull lower lid, instil, close eye, press inner corner; do not touch tip | Discard 4 weeks after opening |
| Ear drops | Warm in hand, tilt head, instil, stay tilted for a few minutes | Cool place |
| Suppositories | Remove wrapper, insert pointed end first; lie down for a few minutes | Cool place (melt in heat) |
| Transdermal patch | Clean, dry, hairless skin; rotate sites; fold used patch and discard safely | Room temperature |

## Result

The correct use and storage of common dosage forms and special devices were studied and demonstrated.

## Precautions

1. Use placebo or demonstration devices only.
2. Never share insulin pens or needles between patients.
3. Check expiry dates and storage instructions.

## Viva questions

1. **Why rinse the mouth after a steroid inhaler?** To prevent oral candidiasis (thrush) and hoarseness.
2. **Advantage of a spacer?** No need to coordinate pressing and breathing; more drug reaches the lungs.
3. **Why prime an insulin pen?** To remove air and make sure the needle is clear, so the full dose is given.
4. **Storage of unopened insulin?** 2–8 °C in a refrigerator, not frozen.
5. **MDI vs DPI inhalation?** MDI: slow, deep breath; DPI: fast, deep breath.
practicals.title: Use and storage of dosage forms, inhalers and insulin pens

# Quality control tests of common dosage forms

**Aim:** To demonstrate quality control tests and evaluation of tablets, capsules, emulsions and sterile injections as per the monographs.

## Principle

Pharmacopoeial tests check that each batch has uniform dose, releases the drug properly and is physically acceptable. Simple tests such as weight variation, hardness, friability, disintegration, emulsion type, clarity and leakage can be done in the laboratory.

## Requirements

Tablets, capsules, emulsion, ampoules; balance, hardness tester (Monsanto), Roche friabilator, disintegration apparatus, water bath, dye solution, black and white inspection board, vacuum desiccator.

## A. Tablets

**1. Uniformity of weight:** weigh 20 tablets together and individually; calculate the average and the % deviation of each.

```text
% deviation = (individual weight − average weight) ÷ average weight × 100
```

IP limits: ≤80 mg ±10%; 80–250 mg ±7.5%; ≥250 mg ±5%. Not more than 2 outside the limit and none outside double the limit.

**2. Hardness:** place a tablet between the anvils of the Monsanto tester and turn the screw until it breaks; read the force (kg). Test 5–10 tablets.

**3. Friability:** take tablets of about 6.5 g (or 10 tablets if each weighs more than 650 mg), dedust, weigh (W1); rotate 100 times at 25 rpm; dedust and weigh (W2).

```text
% friability = (W1 − W2) ÷ W1 × 100        Limit: not more than 1%
```

**4. Disintegration:** one tablet in each of the 6 tubes; water at 37 ± 2 °C; run the apparatus; note the time when no residue remains on the mesh. Uncoated: within 15 minutes.

## B. Capsules

1. **Uniformity of weight:** weigh 20 intact capsules individually, empty each, weigh the shells, find the content weight; limits ±10% (below 300 mg), ±7.5% (300 mg or more).
2. **Disintegration:** as for tablets (discs if specified); limit 30 minutes.

## C. Emulsion

1. **Type tests:** dilution test, dye test (amaranth/methylene blue), conductivity test.
2. **Stability:** keep a sample in a cylinder and note creaming or separation over days; centrifuge test.
3. **Globule size:** observe under a microscope.

## D. Sterile injections (ampoules)

1. **Clarity test:** hold each ampoule against black and white backgrounds under good light, swirl gently and check for particles.
2. **Leakage test:** dip ampoules (tips down) in a dye solution (e.g. 1% methylene blue) in a vacuum desiccator; apply and release vacuum; leaking ampoules become coloured and are rejected.
3. **pH and fill volume** as per monograph. (Sterility and pyrogen/endotoxin tests are demonstrated or explained.)

## Observations

| Product | Test | Result | Limit | Complies? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tablet | Weight variation | | | |
| Tablet | Hardness | | | |
| Tablet | Friability | | ≤1% | |
| Tablet | Disintegration | | 15 min | |
| Capsule | Weight variation | | | |
| Emulsion | Type | | | |
| Injection | Clarity / leakage | | | |

## Result

The given dosage forms were evaluated and found to comply / not comply with the specified limits.

## Precautions

1. Dedust tablets before friability weighing.
2. Maintain 37 ± 2 °C in the disintegration bath.
3. Use calibrated balances and instruments.

## Viva questions

1. **Official tests for tablets?** Uniformity of weight, content uniformity, disintegration, dissolution, assay.
2. **Non-official tests?** Hardness, friability, thickness.
3. **Media for sterility test?** Fluid thioglycollate and soybean–casein digest media.
4. **What does the LAL test detect?** Bacterial endotoxins.
5. **Why leakage test only for ampoules?** Ampoules are sealed by fusion; a tiny crack lets contamination in.
practicals.title: Quality control tests of common dosage forms

questions.answer:
1. Definition: a pharmacopoeia is a legally recognised book of standards for drugs and their preparations, published under government authority; it gives standards of identity, purity and strength and the tests for them.
2. IP is published by the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad (Ministry of Health and Family Welfare); first edition 1955, latest 2022; official under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.
3. Salient features: (a) published in volumes; (b) general notices explain terms (storage, solubility, 'about', constant weight); (c) general chapters/appendices give official test methods – disintegration, dissolution, uniformity of weight, sterility, bacterial endotoxins, limit tests, sieves and powder grades; (d) monographs of drug substances and dosage forms; (e) special monographs for vaccines and immunological products, blood products, herbal products, radiopharmaceuticals and veterinary products; (f) SI units and modern instrumental methods (HPLC, UV, IR); (g) addenda published between editions.
4. Each monograph gives: name, structure, formula, definition with content limits, description, solubility, identification, tests for purity, assay, storage and labelling.
