questions.answer:
1. Ancient period: Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani – physician (vaidya/hakim) prepared and gave medicines; Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas describe drug preparation.
2. British period: imported medicines, chemist shops in port cities (Bathgate and Co., Calcutta, 1811); on-the-job trained compounders.
3. Industry: Acharya P. C. Ray founded Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works (company in 1901); after independence Hindustan Antibiotics and IDPL; Patents Act 1970 helped Indian generic industry grow.
4. Chopra Committee (1930–31) recommended drug control law, national pharmacopoeia and trained, registered pharmacists → Drugs Act 1940, Pharmacy Act 1948, PCI 1949, IP 1955.
5. Education: Prof. M. L. Schroff started pharmacy at BHU in 1932 (father of pharmacy education in India); PCI Education Regulations for D.Pharm, now ER-2020; B.Pharm, M.Pharm, Pharm.D.
6. Practice: community, hospital and clinical pharmacy; Pharmacy Practice Regulations 2015.
7. Associations: IPA, IPCA, APTI, IHPA, IPGA, AIOCD.
questions.question: Write a note on the history of the profession of pharmacy in India.

questions.answer:
Career: 1. Community pharmacy – retail pharmacist or own medical store with a drug licence. 2. Hospital pharmacist – procurement, storage, dispensing, drug information. 3. Government service – health centres, dispensaries, railways, armed forces. 4. Industry – production, packing, QC, stores. 5. Marketing – medical representative. 6. Wholesale distribution. 7. Higher studies – lateral entry to B.Pharm, then M.Pharm/Pharm.D. 8. Regulatory jobs with further qualification.
Associations (with role): Indian Pharmaceutical Association (oldest national body, journal IJPS); Indian Pharmaceutical Congress Association (yearly Indian Pharmaceutical Congress); APTI (teachers, education quality); Indian Hospital Pharmacists' Association; Indian Pharmacy Graduates' Association; AIOCD (chemists and druggists' trade body); internationally FIP. State Pharmacy Councils register pharmacists (statutory).
Qualities: honesty, accuracy, communication, updated knowledge, ethics.
questions.question: Write about pharmacy as a career and the professional associations of pharmacy in India.

questions.answer:
1. IP: Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad; first 1955, latest 2022; official standards in India under Drugs and Cosmetics Act.
2. BP: British Pharmacopoeia Commission; first 1864; now revised yearly; includes European Pharmacopoeia monographs.
3. USP: United States Pharmacopeial Convention; first 1820; standards for drug substances and products.
4. NF: National Formulary, first 1888 by the American Pharmaceutical Association; mainly excipient standards; now published together as USP–NF.
5. Extra Pharmacopoeia (Martindale): first compiled by William Martindale in 1883; now 'Martindale: The Complete Drug Reference' (Royal Pharmaceutical Society); not an official book of standards – gives uses, doses, adverse effects, interactions and proprietary names of drugs from many countries.
Difference: pharmacopoeia = standards; formulary = formulas; Martindale = information.
questions.question: Give a brief introduction to IP, BP, USP, NF and Extra Pharmacopoeia.

questions.answer:
Pharmacopoeia: legal book of standards; gives identity, purity, strength tests and assay; e.g. IP, BP, USP.
Formulary: book of formulas of preparations and prescribing information; e.g. NF, National Formulary of India.
Pharmacopoeia is official for quality control; formulary guides prescribing and compounding.
questions.question: Differentiate between pharmacopoeia and formulary.

questions.answer:
A monograph is the official entry for one drug or preparation in a pharmacopoeia.
Contents: title, structure and formula, molecular weight, definition with limits of content, description, solubility, identification tests, tests for purity (impurity limits, loss on drying, sulphated ash, heavy metals), assay, storage and labelling.
questions.question: What is a monograph? List its contents.

questions.answer:
Drugs Enquiry Committee, 1930–31, chaired by Col. R. N. Chopra.
Found poor-quality and adulterated drugs on sale and no control over pharmacists.
Recommended: a law to control drugs (→ Drugs Act 1940), an Indian pharmacopoeia (→ IP 1955), training and registration of pharmacists (→ Pharmacy Act 1948, PCI 1949), and testing laboratories.
questions.question: Write the role of the Chopra Committee in the development of pharmacy in India.

questions.answer:
Set up in 1949 under the Pharmacy Act, 1948.
Prescribes minimum standards of pharmacy education (Education Regulations, e.g. ER-2020).
Approves courses and institutions; inspects them.
Maintains central register of pharmacists with State Councils; frames regulations like Pharmacy Practice Regulations 2015.
questions.question: Write the functions of the Pharmacy Council of India.

questions.answer: Prof. M. L. Schroff, who started a pharmacy course at Banaras Hindu University in 1932.
questions.question: Who is known as the father of pharmacy education in India?

questions.answer: Martindale: The Complete Drug Reference, first compiled by William Martindale (1883); a reference book of drug information, not an official book of standards.
questions.question: What is the Extra Pharmacopoeia?

questions.answer:
Glass: mainly silica with sodium, calcium and other oxides; boric oxide gives borosilicate.
Types: Type I borosilicate – most resistant, for all injections; Type II soda-lime with treated (de-alkalised) surface – buffered aqueous injections with pH below 7; Type III ordinary soda-lime – dry powders and non-aqueous injections; Type NP – non-parenteral products. Amber glass protects from light.
Advantages: transparent, inert (good grades), impermeable to gases and moisture, rigid, heat-sterilisable, easy to clean, can be coloured.
Disadvantages: brittle, heavy (high transport cost), soda-lime glass releases alkali, may shed flakes, glass pieces dangerous.
Tests: powdered glass test, water attack test, light transmission test.
questions.question: Classify glass used for pharmaceutical containers. Give the advantages and disadvantages of glass as a packaging material.

questions.answer:
Plastics are polymers with additives (plasticisers, stabilisers, fillers).
Examples: polyethylene (LDPE, HDPE) – bottles; polypropylene – closures, autoclavable; PVC – blisters, IV bags; polystyrene – ointment jars; PET – oral liquid bottles; polycarbonate – strong containers.
Advantages: light, unbreakable, flexible, cheap, easily moulded, squeeze bottles and unit doses possible.
Disadvantages (drug–plastic interactions): permeation of gases, moisture, volatile oils; leaching of additives (plasticiser from PVC); sorption of drug or preservative; chemical reaction; modification (oils soften PE); many cannot be heat-sterilised; often not transparent.
questions.question: Discuss plastics as packaging materials with their advantages and disadvantages.

questions.answer:
Definition: substances added to prevent or slow microbial growth in a product during storage and use (antioxidants prevent chemical spoilage).
Ideal properties: broad spectrum at low concentration; non-toxic, non-irritant; stable over shelf life and pH range; compatible with ingredients and container; colourless, odourless, tasteless.
Classification: acids and salts – benzoic acid, sodium benzoate (about 0.1–0.2%), sorbic acid (acid pH); parabens – methyl and propyl (0.18% + 0.02% in injections); alcohols – ethanol (15–20%), benzyl alcohol, chlorobutanol 0.5%; phenols – phenol 0.5%, cresol 0.3%, chlorocresol 0.1%; quaternary ammonium – benzalkonium chloride 0.01% (eye drops), cetrimide; organomercurials – phenylmercuric nitrate 0.002%, thiomersal.
Antioxidants: BHA, BHT, tocopherol (oil); ascorbic acid, sodium metabisulphite (water); EDTA as synergist.
questions.question: Define preservatives. Write the ideal properties and classify antimicrobial preservatives with examples.

questions.answer:
Colours: purpose – attractiveness, identification, match flavour. Natural (chlorophyll, carotene, cochineal, caramel), mineral (iron oxides, titanium dioxide), synthetic coal-tar dyes (tartrazine, sunset yellow, amaranth, erythrosine, brilliant blue), lakes (dyes on aluminium hydroxide, for coatings).
Flavours: mask taste; four basic tastes – salty (butterscotch, apricot, liquorice), bitter (chocolate, mint, anise, wild cherry), sour (citrus, raspberry), sweet (vanilla, fruit). Natural (volatile oils, juices) and synthetic (vanillin, methyl salicylate).
Sweeteners: sucrose, glucose, sorbitol, mannitol, glycerin; artificial – saccharin (300–500×), aspartame (about 200×, avoid in phenylketonuria), sucralose (about 600×), acesulfame K, stevia.
questions.question: Write a note on organoleptic agents: colouring, flavouring and sweetening agents.

questions.answer:
Metals (tin, aluminium, tin-plated steel): uses – collapsible tubes, aerosol cans, foils, caps. Advantages – impermeable to light, moisture and gas; strong; light (Al); tubes do not let air back in. Disadvantages – costly, may corrode or react (need lacquer lining), opaque, dent easily, lead is toxic.
Rubber (natural, butyl, neoprene, nitrile, silicone): uses – vial stoppers, dropper bulbs, plungers. Advantages – elastic, seals well, reseals after needle puncture. Disadvantages – sorption of preservatives, leaching of additives, gas and moisture permeability, ageing, coring. Remedy – wash, boil and pre-soak closures in the preservative solution; use coated closures.
questions.question: Write the advantages and disadvantages of metal and rubber as packaging materials.

questions.answer:
Compatible – no reaction, leaching or sorption.
Protects from light, moisture, air and microbes.
Strong enough for handling and transport.
Non-toxic and does not change taste or odour.
Withstands sterilisation if needed; suits dosage form and route.
Economical, printable, meets legal standards.
questions.question: Write the selection criteria for packaging materials.

questions.answer:
Permeation – passage of gas, water vapour, volatile ingredients through the wall.
Leaching – additives move into the product.
Sorption – drug or preservative taken up by plastic.
Chemical reaction – between product and polymer.
Modification – product changes the plastic (softening, deformation).
questions.question: Explain the problems of drug–plastic interaction.

questions.answer:
Water-soluble: ascorbic acid, sodium metabisulphite, sodium bisulphite, sodium sulphite.
Oil-soluble: BHA, BHT, tocopherols, propyl gallate.
Synergists/chelating agents: disodium edetate, citric acid.
Other measures: nitrogen in head space, amber containers, cool storage.
questions.question: Classify antioxidants with examples.

questions.answer:
Primary – in direct contact with product: bottle, ampoule, vial, strip, blister, tube.
Secondary – holds primary packs: carton with leaflet.
Tertiary – for bulk transport: corrugated box, shipper, pallet.
questions.question: Give the levels of packaging with examples.

questions.answer: Type I (borosilicate) glass, because it is highly resistant and releases very little alkali.
questions.question: Which type of glass is used for parenteral preparations?

questions.answer: Rubber sorbs preservatives from the solution; soaking closures in the preservative first saturates them so the product does not lose its preservative.
questions.question: Why are rubber closures pre-treated with preservative?

questions.answer:
Principle: impact and attrition by balls in a rotating cylinder.
Construction: hollow horizontal cylinder (steel, porcelain or rubber-lined) on a shaft; filled 30–50% with balls of different sizes; material fills gaps.
Working: at low speed balls cascade (attrition only); at optimum speed (about 1/2–2/3 of critical speed) balls are lifted and fall on the material (cataracting) – best grinding; at critical speed balls stick to the wall (centrifuging) – no grinding.
Uses: fine grinding of hard drugs, dyes, pigments; wet or dry milling; sterile and toxic materials in closed system.
Advantages: very fine product, closed system, wet or dry.
Disadvantages: slow, noisy, contamination from ball wear, long cleaning.
Draw the cylinder with balls at three speeds.
questions.question: Describe the principle, construction, working, uses, advantages and disadvantages of a ball mill.

questions.answer:
Principle: impact by high-speed rotating hammers.
Construction: metal casing; central shaft with swinging or fixed hammers; feed hopper at top; screen at bottom to control size.
Working: material fed in; hammers strike and throw particles against casing; particles break until they pass through the screen.
Uses: milling dry granules, crystalline and fibrous drugs, wet masses (knife edges).
Advantages: fast, compact, easy to clean, size controlled by screen and speed, continuous.
Disadvantages: heat generation (not for heat-sensitive/sticky), screen clogging, wear with abrasive material, noise.
questions.question: Explain the principle, construction and working of a hammer mill with a labelled diagram.

questions.answer:
Principle: hot air blown upward through wet granules at a velocity that lifts and suspends them (fluidization); each particle is surrounded by hot air, so drying is rapid.
Construction: product bowl with perforated base; air inlet with fan, filter and heater below; drying chamber above; bag (finger) filters; exhaust fan.
Working: load wet granules → switch on fan and heater → bed fluidizes → water evaporates and leaves with air → fines held by bags → dry in about 20–40 min → unload.
Advantages: fast, uniform, no hot spots, less handling, can also granulate and coat, short heat exposure.
Disadvantages: fines loss, static charge (risk with organic solvents), attrition of granules, unsuitable for sticky materials.
questions.question: Describe the construction and working of a fluidized bed dryer with its advantages and disadvantages.

questions.answer:
Definition: drying by removing water from a frozen product by sublimation under vacuum.
Principle: below the triple point of water (about 0.01 °C, 4.58 mm Hg) ice changes directly to vapour.
Steps: 1. preparation – solution sterile filtered and filled in vials, stoppers half-inserted; 2. freezing – on shelves to well below freezing (about −40 °C); 3. primary drying – vacuum applied, shelves gently heated, ice sublimes, vapour trapped on a very cold condenser; 4. secondary drying – temperature raised to remove bound water; 5. stoppering under vacuum/nitrogen and sealing.
Parts: chamber with shelves, refrigeration, condenser, vacuum pump.
Uses: antibiotics, vaccines, proteins, plasma. Advantages: heat-sensitive products, porous cake dissolves fast, long shelf life. Disadvantages: costly, long cycle, skilled operation.
questions.question: What is freeze drying? Describe the principle and steps of the process.

questions.answer:
IP grades: coarse – all through sieve 10, not more than 40% through 44; moderately coarse 22/60; moderately fine 44/85; fine – all through 85; very fine – all through 120. Sieve number = meshes per inch; e.g. sieve 10 = 1700 µm, 85 = 180 µm.
Cyclone separator – principle: centrifugal force.
Construction: vertical cylinder with conical bottom; tangential inlet at top; central air outlet pipe at top; solids outlet at cone bottom.
Working: air with particles enters tangentially and spirals down; heavier particles thrown to wall and slide to the bottom outlet; air with fines turns up and leaves through central pipe.
Uses: collecting product from spray/fluid bed dryers, dust collection. Advantages: no moving parts, cheap, continuous. Disadvantages: poor for very fine particles, wall wear.
questions.question: Give the IP classification of powders. Describe the construction and working of a cyclone separator.

questions.answer:
Definition: separation of solids from a fluid by passing it through a porous medium; filtrate passes, cake remains.
Mechanisms: straining, impingement, entanglement, attraction.
Darcy's law: rate = dV/dt = K A ΔP / (η L), where A = area, ΔP = pressure difference, η = viscosity, L = thickness of medium and cake, K = permeability.
Factors: larger area and higher pressure increase rate; higher viscosity slows (warm the liquid); thick cake slows; larger pores faster but less clear; filter aids (kieselguhr) keep cake porous.
Applications: clarification of syrups and elixirs, sterilisation of heat-sensitive solutions (0.22 µm), particle removal from injections, HEPA air filtration.
questions.question: Define filtration. Explain the theory of filtration and the factors affecting the rate of filtration.

questions.answer:
Definition: separation of active soluble constituents of crude drugs from inert material using a solvent (menstruum); residue = marc.
Methods: infusion, decoction, digestion, maceration, percolation, continuous hot extraction (Soxhlet), modern (supercritical CO2, microwave, ultrasound).
Maceration: drug + whole menstruum in a closed vessel for 7 days with frequent shaking; strain, press marc, combine, filter. For soft and unorganised drugs.
Percolation: moistened drug packed in a percolator; menstruum passes slowly downward; percolate collected; marc pressed. For potent drugs, tinctures and liquid extracts.
Applications: tinctures, extracts, isolation of alkaloids, glycosides, oils.
questions.question: Define extraction. Classify methods of extraction and describe maceration and percolation.

questions.answer:
Increases surface area → faster dissolution and absorption.
Uniform mixing and dose.
Faster extraction of crude drugs.
Faster drying.
Better stability of suspensions and emulsions.
Better flow and filling.
questions.question: Write the objectives (applications) of size reduction.

questions.answer:
Principle: tumbling (diffusive mixing).
Construction: two cones joined at bases by a short cylinder, rotating on a horizontal shaft; loading/discharge port; filled 50–60%.
Working: rotates about 30–100 rpm; powder falls from one cone to the other repeatedly.
Uses: gentle blending of free-flowing powders, lubrication. Demerit: segregation of powders differing in size/density.
questions.question: Describe the double cone blender.

questions.answer:
Principle: shear between three rollers rotating at different speeds.
Construction: three adjustable horizontal rollers, each faster than the previous; scraper on the last.
Working: material fed between first two rollers, sheared in each gap, scraped off the third.
Use: smooth ointments and pastes. Demerit: heat; loss of volatiles.
questions.question: Write the principle and working of a triple roller mill.

questions.answer:
Principle: high shear in rotor–stator head.
Rotor at high speed sucks material in, mills it in the rotor–stator gap and expels it through stator holes; cycle repeats.
Uses: emulsions, creams, lotions, fine suspensions, dissolving gums.
Merits: fine droplets, fast. Demerits: heat, air entrapment.
questions.question: Write a note on the Silverson mixer homogenizer.

questions.answer:
Membrane: thin cellulose ester/nylon/PTFE film; uniform pores 0.1–10 µm; 0.22 µm sterilises; clogs easily, disposable.
Sintered glass: fused borosilicate glass particles; grades 1 (coarse) to 5 (fine, retains bacteria); chemically resistant (not HF, hot alkali); reusable, brittle, costly, hard to clean.
questions.question: Compare membrane filters and sintered glass filters.

questions.answer:
Principle: high-speed turbine impeller produces radial and tangential flow with shear.
Construction: vessel, central shaft with turbine blades on a disc, motor, baffles.
Working: liquid thrown outward, circulates up and down and back to centre.
Uses: low–medium viscosity liquids, solutions, emulsions. Demerit: foaming, vortex without baffles.
questions.question: Write the principle and working of a turbine mixer.

questions.answer: The speed at which the balls just remain stuck to the wall of the mill throughout rotation due to centrifugal force; no grinding then. Optimum speed is about half to two-thirds of it.
questions.question: What is critical speed of a ball mill?

questions.answer: Menstruum: the solvent used for extraction. Marc: the insoluble residue left after extraction.
questions.question: Define menstruum and marc.

questions.answer:
Definition: solid unit dosage forms of drug with or without excipients made by compressing powder or granules.
Granulation reasons: flow, compressibility, no segregation, less dust.
Steps: 1. weighing and sieving drug and excipients; 2. dry mixing (diluent, part of disintegrant); 3. wet massing with binder solution (starch paste, PVP); 4. wet screening (sieve 8–12); 5. drying (tray dryer or FBD); 6. dry screening (sieve 16–20); 7. lubrication – add lubricant, glidant, extra-granular disintegrant and blend; 8. compression on single punch or rotary press.
Merits: good flow and compression, uniform distribution. Demerits: many steps, heat and moisture.
Mention: dry granulation (slugging/roller compaction) for moisture-sensitive drugs; direct compression for suitable materials.
questions.question: Define tablets. Describe the steps of tablet manufacture by wet granulation.

questions.answer:
Capping: top separates as a cap – air trapped, excess fines, dry granules, worn punches, high speed → more binder, correct moisture, remove fines, precompression, slower speed, check tooling.
Lamination: splits into layers – same causes plus excess lubricant → reduce lubricant, slower speed.
Picking: material pulled off by punch face, especially at lettering – moisture, low-melting ingredients → dry granules, add antiadherent (talc, colloidal silica), chrome-plated punches, larger letters.
Sticking: granules adhere to die/punch – moisture, low lubricant, rough punches → dry granules, more lubricant, polish punches.
Mottling: uneven colour – colour migration on drying, coloured drug → use lakes, change solvent, reduce particle size.
Also: chipping, cracking, double impression, weight variation.
questions.question: Explain tablet defects – capping, lamination, picking, sticking and mottling – with causes and remedies.

questions.answer:
Official: 1. uniformity of weight – 20 tablets; IP limits ≤80 mg ±10%, 80–250 mg ±7.5%, ≥250 mg ±5%; ≤2 outside limit, none outside double. 2. Content uniformity – low-dose tablets. 3. Disintegration – 6-tube basket, 37 ± 2 °C, 28–32 cycles/min; uncoated 15 min, film 30 min, sugar 60 min, dispersible 3 min; enteric intact 2 h in 0.1 M HCl then disintegrates within 60 min in pH 6.8 buffer. 4. Dissolution – 900 ml, 37 ± 0.5 °C, basket 100 rpm or paddle 50 rpm. 5. Assay.
Non-official: hardness (Monsanto/Pfizer, about 4–6 kg); friability (Roche friabilator, 25 rpm, 4 min, 100 revolutions; loss ≤1%; % = (W1 − W2)/W1 × 100); thickness and diameter (vernier/micrometer).
questions.question: Describe the official and non-official evaluation tests for tablets.

questions.answer:
Classification: oral – compressed, multiple compressed (layered, compression-coated), sugar-, film- and enteric-coated, chewable, effervescent, dispersible, soluble; oral cavity – buccal, sublingual, lozenges; others – vaginal tablets, implants.
Modified release: time or site of release changed.
Delayed release – enteric-coated (aspirin, pantoprazole).
Sustained/extended release – slow release over a long time, once or twice daily dosing (diclofenac SR, metformin ER).
Controlled release – planned, near-constant rate (osmotic tablets).
Fast dissolving/ODT – disintegrate on tongue in seconds without water (ondansetron ODT).
Multi-layered – immediate + sustained layers or incompatible drugs.
Merits: fewer doses, steady levels, compliance. Demerits: cost, cannot crush (dose dumping), inflexible dose.
questions.question: Classify tablets. Write a note on modified-release tablets.

questions.answer:
Shell: gelatin, water (13–16%), colour, titanium dioxide, preservative.
Manufacture (dipping): pins dipped in warm gelatin → spun for even film → dried with cool air → stripped → trimmed → cap and body joined (locking rings), printed.
Fill: drug + diluent (lactose, MCC; avoid calcium salts with tetracycline) + glidant + lubricant.
Filling: hand (punch method), capsule filling board (100/300 holes: separate, fill, level, rejoin), automatic machines (dosator or tamping disc); then dedust and polish.
Sizes: 000 (about 1.37 ml, largest) to 5 (about 0.13 ml); 0 about 0.68 ml, 1 about 0.50 ml.
Gelatin types: A (acid, pI 7–9), B (alkaline, pI 4.7–5).
questions.question: Describe the manufacture of hard gelatin capsule shells and their filling. Add a note on capsule sizes.

questions.answer:
Soft gelatin capsules: one-piece hermetically sealed elastic shells.
Shell: gelatin + plasticiser (glycerin, sorbitol, propylene glycol) + water + colour, opacifier, preservative.
Fills: oils and oily solutions (vitamins A, D, E), suspensions in oil, PEG solutions; avoid much water, extreme pH.
Manufacture: plate process; rotary die process (two gelatin ribbons between rotating dies, fill injected via wedge, sealed and cut together); reciprocating die; Accogel (powders).
Evaluation of capsules: weight variation (IP <300 mg ±10%, ≥300 mg ±7.5%), disintegration (30 min), dissolution (with sinkers), content uniformity, assay, moisture, leak test (soft), visual inspection.
questions.question: Write about soft gelatin capsules: composition, fill materials, manufacture and evaluation of capsules.

questions.answer:
Reasons for coating: mask taste/odour, protect from light/moisture/air, enteric protection, controlled release, appearance, identification.
Sugar coating steps: sealing (shellac/CAP) → subcoating (syrup + gelatin/acacia + talc/CaCO3) → smoothing (syrup) → colouring → polishing (waxes) → printing.
Film coating: polymer (HPMC, methylcellulose, ethylcellulose), plasticiser (PEG, propylene glycol), colourant/opacifier, solvent (water/organic), sprayed in perforated pan; 20–100 µm.
Enteric polymers: CAP, HPMCP, PVAP, methacrylic copolymers (Eudragit L/S), shellac.
Comparison: film – fast, 2–3% weight gain, logo visible, automated; sugar – slow (days), large weight gain, elegant, needs skill.
questions.question: Describe sugar coating and film coating of tablets and compare them.

questions.answer:
Diluent – bulk: lactose, MCC, starch, dicalcium phosphate.
Binder – cohesion: starch paste, PVP, gelatin, acacia.
Disintegrant – break-up: starch, croscarmellose, crospovidone, sodium starch glycolate.
Lubricant – reduces die-wall friction: magnesium stearate.
Glidant – flow: colloidal silica, talc.
Antiadherent – prevents sticking: talc.
Colours, flavours, sweeteners.
questions.question: List tablet excipients with their functions and examples.

questions.answer:
Apparatus: Roche friabilator (drum with a curved baffle).
Sample: tablets weighing about 6.5 g (unit weight ≤650 mg) or 10 tablets (>650 mg), dedusted and weighed (W1).
Rotate 25 rpm for 4 min (100 revolutions); dedust and reweigh (W2).
% friability = (W1 − W2)/W1 × 100; limit not more than 1%.
questions.question: Describe the friability test for tablets.

questions.answer:
1. Filling – lower punch drops, feed shoe fills die.
2. Scraping/weight adjustment – feed shoe moves away levelling granules.
3. Compression – upper punch descends and compresses.
4. Ejection – upper punch rises, lower punch pushes tablet up.
5. Push-off – feed shoe sweeps tablet away and refills die.
questions.question: Write the compression cycle of a single punch tablet machine.

questions.answer:
Wet: binder liquid, drying; good for most drugs; many steps, heat/moisture.
Dry (slugging/roller compaction): no liquid or heat; for moisture/heat-sensitive drugs; dusty.
Direct compression: blend and compress; fewest steps; needs directly compressible excipients (MCC, spray-dried lactose); segregation risk.
questions.question: Compare wet granulation, dry granulation and direct compression.

questions.answer:
Advantages: tasteless shell masks taste, easy to swallow, rapid release, fewer excipients, liquids in softgels, easy identification.
Disadvantages: not for very soluble irritant salts, efflorescent or deliquescent drugs; humidity-sensitive; animal origin of gelatin; sometimes costlier.
questions.question: Write the advantages and disadvantages of capsules.

questions.answer: Uncoated tablets: 15 minutes; film-coated tablets: 30 minutes (at 37 ± 2 °C).
questions.question: What is the disintegration time limit for uncoated and film-coated tablets as per IP?

questions.answer: Calcium forms a complex (chelate) with tetracycline and reduces its absorption.
questions.question: Why are calcium-containing diluents avoided in tetracycline capsules?

questions.answer:
Definition: thermodynamically unstable system of two immiscible liquids, one dispersed as globules in the other, stabilised by an emulsifying agent.
Types: o/w, w/o, multiple (w/o/w, o/w/o).
Tests: dilution (o/w dilutes with water), dye test (water-soluble dye colours continuous phase in o/w), conductivity (o/w conducts), fluorescence (w/o whole field fluoresces).
Emulsifying agents: acacia, tragacanth, gelatin, wool fat, bentonite, soaps, Spans (w/o), Tweens (o/w); HLB.
Preparation: dry gum method (gum + oil, add water at once, triturate to click); wet gum method (mucilage first, oil added slowly); bottle method (volatile oils). Primary emulsion ratio oil:water:gum – fixed oil 4:2:1, volatile 2:2:1, mineral 3:2:1.
questions.question: Define emulsion. Give its types, tests for identification and methods of preparation.

questions.answer:
Creaming: globules rise or sink to form a concentrated layer; reversible by shaking.
Cracking/breaking: globules coalesce, phases separate; irreversible; caused by wrong emulsifier, temperature extremes, microbes, incompatible additives.
Phase inversion: o/w ↔ w/o, due to phase volume change or emulsifier change (e.g. calcium ions).
Microbial growth: add preservatives.
Stokes' law: v = 2r²(ρ1 − ρ2)g/9η; reduce creaming by small globules (homogenise), high viscosity of continuous phase (thickeners), small density difference.
Evaluation: globule size, viscosity, phase separation on storage and centrifugation, pH, microbial limits.
questions.question: Discuss the stability problems of emulsions and the factors affecting them (Stokes' law).

questions.answer:
Definition: coarse dispersion of insoluble finely divided solid in a liquid vehicle.
Reasons: insoluble drug, taste masking, stability, depot injections, external use.
Good suspension: slow settling, easily redispersed, no cake, pours easily, uniform dose.
Flocculated: loose flocs, fast settling, large loose sediment, easy redispersion, clear supernatant quickly.
Deflocculated: separate particles, slow settling, compact sediment forms hard cake, cloudy supernatant.
Ingredients: wetting agents, suspending agents (tragacanth, CMC, bentonite, xanthan), flocculating agents, buffers, preservatives.
Evaluation: sedimentation volume F = Hu/Ho, redispersibility, particle size, viscosity. Label 'Shake well before use'.
questions.question: Define suspension. Write the properties of a good suspension and compare flocculated and deflocculated suspensions.

questions.answer:
Definition: soft semisolid preparation for external application to skin or mucous membranes.
Bases: oleaginous (soft/hard/liquid paraffin, vegetable oils – occlusive, greasy); absorption (wool fat, wool alcohols, beeswax – take up water); emulsion w/o (cold cream) and o/w (emulsifying ointment, aqueous cream – washable); water-soluble (PEG).
Ideal base: inert, non-irritant, stable, compatible, easy to apply and remove, releases drug.
Methods: trituration/incorporation (levigate insoluble powder with base on slab – sulphur ointment); fusion (melt in descending order of melting point, stir till cool – simple ointment); emulsification.
Add a note on creams (o/w vanishing, w/o cold) and pastes (high solids).
questions.question: Define ointment. Classify ointment bases and describe methods of preparation of ointments.

questions.answer:
Suppositories: solid forms for rectum (also vagina, urethra) that melt or dissolve to give local or systemic action; adult rectal about 2 g. Pessaries: vaginal, larger (about 3–8 g).
Uses: laxative (glycerin), haemorrhoids, antifungal; systemic when oral route impossible (paracetamol, antiemetics).
Bases: fatty – theobroma oil (melts 30–35 °C; polymorphism, so melt gently below about 36 °C), hard fat; water-soluble – glycerinated gelatin (pessaries), PEG; emulsifying bases.
Displacement value: parts by weight of drug that displace one part of base; used to calculate base needed for medicated suppositories.
Preparation: hand rolling, fusion/pour moulding (melt base, mix drug, pour into lubricated mould, cool, trim, remove), compression moulding.
Evaluation: weight uniformity, melting range, disintegration, hardness, content.
questions.question: Write about suppositories and pessaries: definition, bases, displacement value and method of preparation.

questions.answer:
Syrup: concentrated viscous sweet aqueous solution of sucrose (simple syrup 66.7% w/w IP; USP 85% w/v); medicated or flavoured.
Preparation: solution with heat (risk of inversion and caramelisation), agitation without heat, percolation, addition of sucrose to medicated liquid.
Syrup merits: pleasant, masks taste, soothing, self-preserving when concentrated. Demerits: not for diabetics, caries, crystallisation, fermentation if dilute.
Elixir: clear sweetened hydroalcoholic solution; alcohol aids solubility and preservation; e.g. piperazine citrate elixir. Merits: clear, stable. Demerits: alcohol not suited for children, less taste masking, volatile loss.
questions.question: Define syrups and elixirs. Give their advantages, disadvantages and methods of preparation of syrups.

questions.answer:
Nasal: drops, sprays, powders, ointments/gels, washes; local or systemic. Formulation – aqueous, isotonic, pH about 5.5–6.5, buffer, benzalkonium chloride in multi-dose, viscosity agents; avoid oily drops (lipid pneumonia). Examples: saline drops, xylometazoline, fluticasone spray, desmopressin.
Ear: drops (solutions/suspensions), washes, ointments, powders. Vehicles – water, glycerin, propylene glycol (viscous, hygroscopic), alcohol, oils. Uses – wax softeners (sodium bicarbonate ear drops, olive oil), antibacterial, antifungal, analgesic. Warm to body temperature; sterile preparations if eardrum perforated.
questions.question: Write notes on nasal and ear preparations.

questions.answer:
Liniments: applied with friction; oily/alcoholic/soapy; counter-irritant, rubefacient for muscle pain; not on broken skin; e.g. turpentine liniment, white liniment.
Lotions: applied without friction; mostly aqueous; cooling, soothing, protective; e.g. calamine lotion.
questions.question: Differentiate between liniments and lotions.

questions.answer:
o/w: oil dispersed in water; dilutes with water; conducts electricity; non-greasy, washable; oral and IV use; emulsifier HLB about 8–18 (Tweens).
w/o: water dispersed in oil; does not dilute with water; does not conduct; greasy; external (cold cream); emulsifier HLB about 3–6 (Spans).
questions.question: Differentiate between o/w and w/o emulsions.

questions.answer:
For drugs unstable in water (amoxicillin, ampicillin, cefalexin).
Supplied as dry powder/granules; water added to the mark before dispensing/use.
Long shelf life dry; use within stated time (about 7–14 days), often refrigerated.
Label: volume of water, shake well, storage, discard date.
questions.question: Write a note on dry powders for reconstitution.

questions.answer:
Pastes: stiff semisolids with high proportion (often ≥50%) of powder; less greasy, stay in place, absorb secretions; e.g. zinc oxide paste.
Gels: liquid held in 3-D network of gelling agent (sodium alginate, carbomer, methylcellulose, tragacanth); non-greasy, cooling; e.g. lubricant jelly, diclofenac gel.
questions.question: Define pastes and gels with examples.

questions.answer:
Appearance, clarity, colour, odour.
pH, viscosity, specific gravity.
Alcohol content (elixirs).
Globule/particle size, creaming/sedimentation and redispersibility (emulsions, suspensions).
Microbial limits, preservative content, assay, fill volume.
questions.question: Write the evaluation tests for liquid oral preparations.

questions.answer: 66.7% w/w sucrose (the USP simple syrup is 85% w/v).
questions.question: What is the concentration of sucrose in Simple Syrup IP?

questions.answer: 4 : 2 : 1 (oil : water : gum).
questions.question: What is the ratio of oil, water and gum in the primary emulsion of a fixed oil?

questions.answer: The number of parts by weight of a drug that displaces one part by weight of the suppository base.
questions.question: Define displacement value.

questions.answer:
Definition: sterile preparations for injection, infusion or implantation, bypassing the alimentary canal.
Routes: IV, IM, SC, ID, intrathecal, intra-articular.
Types: solutions, suspensions, emulsions, dry powders for reconstitution; LVP and SVP.
Advantages: rapid action, for unconscious/vomiting patients, for drugs destroyed orally (insulin), depot effect, fluid and nutrition.
Disadvantages: pain, trained personnel, irreversible once given, infection, cost.
Additives: vehicle – Water for Injections; non-aqueous – fixed oils, ethyl oleate, PEG, propylene glycol; tonicity agents (NaCl, dextrose); buffers (phosphate, citrate); preservatives (benzyl alcohol, chlorocresol, phenol, parabens) for multi-dose; antioxidants (metabisulphite, ascorbic acid, nitrogen); chelators (EDTA).
Requirements: sterile, pyrogen-free, particle-free, isotonic, stable.
questions.question: Define parenteral preparations. Write their types, advantages, disadvantages and formulation additives.

questions.answer:
Production: clean-room (Grade A filling); containers washed, rinsed with WFI, dry-heat sterilised/depyrogenated; solution prepared in WFI, pH adjusted; clarified and 0.22 µm filtered; filled under laminar air flow; ampoules sealed, vials stoppered and crimped; terminal sterilisation (autoclave 121 °C, 15 min) if heat-stable; QC; labelling and packing.
QC tests: sterility test (fluid thioglycollate and soybean–casein digest media, direct inoculation or membrane filtration – no growth); pyrogen test (rabbit temperature rise); bacterial endotoxin (LAL gel-clot); clarity/particulate matter (visual against black and white, counters); leakage test (dye bath under vacuum for ampoules); extractable volume, pH, assay.
questions.question: Describe the production of injections and the quality control tests for parenterals.

questions.answer:
Vaccines: preparations of antigens that produce active immunity.
Classification: live attenuated (BCG, OPV, measles, MMR); killed/inactivated (IPV, rabies, typhoid, pertussis); toxoids (tetanus, diphtheria); subunit/recombinant (hepatitis B, HPV); conjugate (Hib); combined (DPT, pentavalent).
Bacterial vaccine manufacture: 1. seed lot of selected strain; 2. culture in fermenters in suitable medium; 3. harvest by centrifugation, resuspend in saline; 4. kill by heat/formaldehyde/phenol (killed vaccines); 5. standardise (bacterial count/antigen content); 6. blend – dilute, add preservative and adjuvant; 7. aseptic filling; 8. QC – sterility, safety, potency, identity.
Viral vaccines are grown in embryonated eggs or cell cultures.
Storage 2–8 °C, cold chain.
questions.question: Define vaccines. Classify them and describe the general method of manufacture of bacterial vaccines.

questions.answer:
Toxoid: exotoxin made non-toxic with formaldehyde but still antigenic (active immunity). Manufacture: grow C. tetani/C. diphtheriae in liquid medium → toxin released, bacteria filtered off → formaldehyde + warmth (toxoiding) → purify, concentrate, standardise in Lf units → adsorb on aluminium hydroxide/phosphate (adsorbed toxoid) → preservative, aseptic filling → tests for sterility, non-toxicity, potency.
Antisera: antibody preparations from immunised animals (horses) or humans giving passive immunity; e.g. ATS, anti-diphtheria serum, polyvalent anti-snake venom, immunoglobulins. Manufacture: immunise horses with increasing doses of toxoid/toxin/venom → bleed aseptically → separate plasma → purify (ammonium sulphate, pepsin digestion) → standardise, preservative, sterile filter, fill, freeze-dry if needed → test.
Caution: allergic reactions; sensitivity test dose.
questions.question: Write notes on toxoids and antisera with their methods of manufacture.

questions.answer:
Eye drops: sterile solutions/suspensions for instillation into the eye. Requirements: sterile (Pseudomonas risk), isotonic (0.9% NaCl equivalent), pH near 7.4 (buffered), clear or very fine particles, viscosity agents (methylcellulose, HPMC, PVA), preservative (benzalkonium chloride about 0.01%, chlorhexidine, phenylmercuric salts, chlorobutanol); sterilised by autoclave or 0.22 µm filtration with aseptic filling; dropper containers; discard 4 weeks after opening.
Eye ointments: sterile semisolids; base of yellow soft paraffin, liquid paraffin and wool fat; base melted, filtered and dry-heat sterilised; sterile micronised drug added aseptically; filled in sterile tubes with nozzle; no gritty particles. Longer contact time, but blur vision.
questions.question: Write about eye drops and eye ointments: requirements, formulation and preparation.

questions.answer:
Definition: granules containing acid and bicarbonate that release CO2 when added to water; mask taste.
Reactions: citric acid + 3 NaHCO3 → sodium citrate + 3 CO2 + 4 H2O; tartaric acid + 2 NaHCO3 → sodium tartrate + 2 CO2 + 2 H2O.
Acid mixture: citric alone → sticky mass; tartaric alone → crumbly granules; use citric : tartaric 1 : 2.
Preparation: fusion method – mix powders, heat about 93–104 °C; water of crystallisation of citric acid acts as binder; pass through sieve, dry at not more than 50 °C. Wet method – alcohol as granulating fluid.
Granules vs powder: less hygroscopic, controlled effervescence, better flow.
Pack airtight; label 'Dissolve in water before taking'.
questions.question: What are effervescent granules? Describe their preparation and the reasons for using citric and tartaric acid together.

questions.answer:
Fine powders blown into body cavities (nose, throat, ear, tooth socket) with an insufflator.
Local (antiseptic, decongestant) or systemic action.
Very fine powder for even spread.
Demerits: inaccurate dose, may be inhaled and cause coughing.
Dry powder inhalers are a modern controlled form.
questions.question: Write a note on insufflations.

questions.answer:
Very fine, free from grit; free-flowing; spread easily and adhere to skin.
Inert base: talc, starch, zinc oxide, kaolin, zinc stearate.
Must be sterile if for wounds/broken skin (talc can carry tetanus spores).
Packed in sifter-top containers; label 'For external use only'.
questions.question: Write the requirements of dusting powders.

questions.answer:
Solutions with the same osmotic pressure as body fluids are isotonic; 0.9% NaCl and 5% dextrose are isotonic with blood; freezing point −0.52 °C.
Hypotonic → red cells swell and burst (haemolysis), pain/irritation; hypertonic → cells shrink (crenation), irritation.
Isotonic preparations are comfortable and safe.
questions.question: What is isotonicity? Why is it important for injections and eye drops?

questions.answer:
Moist heat (autoclave) 121 °C for 15 min – aqueous injections, closures.
Dry heat 160 °C for 2 h – glassware, oils, powders.
Filtration 0.22 µm – heat-sensitive solutions.
Ethylene oxide gas – plastics, devices.
Radiation (gamma, electron beam) – disposables, sutures.
questions.question: Write the methods of sterilisation with conditions.

questions.answer:
Active: body produces own antibodies; after infection or vaccination/toxoid; slow onset; long-lasting.
Passive: ready-made antibodies given (sera, antitoxins, immunoglobulins, mother to baby); immediate; short-lived.
questions.question: Differentiate between active and passive immunity.

questions.answer:
Cold chain: system keeping vaccines at the right temperature from manufacturer to patient (walk-in coolers, ice-lined refrigerators, deep freezers, cold boxes, vaccine carriers).
Store most vaccines at 2–8 °C; never freeze adsorbed vaccines (DPT, TT, hepatitis B).
Vaccine vial monitor shows heat exposure.
Protect from light; use reconstituted vaccine within stated time.
questions.question: Write a note on the cold chain and storage of vaccines.

questions.answer: Fluid thioglycollate medium (bacteria, anaerobes) and soybean–casein digest medium (fungi and aerobic bacteria).
questions.question: Name the media used in the sterility test.

questions.answer: A bacterial toxin made non-toxic by formaldehyde treatment but still antigenic; e.g. tetanus toxoid, diphtheria toxoid.
questions.question: What is a toxoid? Give two examples.

questions.answer:
QC: part of GMP concerned with sampling, specifications and testing, and with release procedures ensuring materials/products are not released until quality is satisfactory.
QA: wide concept covering all matters that influence product quality; total of organised arrangements to ensure medicines are of required quality. QA ⊃ GMP ⊃ QC.
Differences: focus – product (QC) vs process/system (QA); nature – reactive/detects vs proactive/prevents; activities – testing, inspection vs SOPs, documentation, audits, validation, training, batch release, recalls; done by QC lab vs QA department/organisation.
QC functions: raw material, packing material, in-process, finished product testing, stability, environmental monitoring.
questions.question: Define quality control and quality assurance. Differentiate between them.

questions.answer:
Definition: part of QA ensuring products are consistently produced and controlled to the quality standards appropriate to their use; 'current' = up-to-date methods. In India – Schedule M of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules.
Requirements: premises (location, one-way flow, smooth cleanable surfaces, separate areas); personnel (qualified, trained, healthy, hygienic, proper clothing); equipment (suitable, stainless steel, calibrated, maintained, status-labelled); processes (validated, SOPs, line clearance, avoid mix-ups and cross-contamination); materials (approved vendors, quarantine, testing, labelling); documentation (master formula, BMR, packing records, specifications); sanitation, pest control; complaints and recalls; self-inspection.
Importance: patient safety, consistency, legal compliance, export.
questions.question: Define GMP. Write the important requirements of cGMP.

questions.answer:
Site: away from pollution; good water, power, transport.
Layout: one-way flow – receipt → quarantine → QC approval → approved store → dispensing → production → in-process control → packaging → QC release → finished goods store → dispatch; separate routes for people, materials, waste; air locks for sterile areas.
Sections: stores (receipt, quarantine, storage, FEFO); dispensing (weighing under dust control); production blocks (tablets, capsules, liquids, externals, sterile; dedicated for β-lactams, hormones, cytotoxics); sterile area (HEPA, Grades A–D); packaging (line clearance); QC lab; QA; engineering/maintenance; utilities (purified water, WFI, steam, HVAC); effluent treatment; administration.
questions.question: Describe the basic layout, sections and activities of a pharmaceutical manufacturing plant.

questions.answer:
Calibration: establishing the relationship between values shown by an instrument and known reference standard values (e.g. balance with standard weights, pH meter with buffers, thermometer with reference thermometer); done at set frequency, status labels, records.
Validation: documented evidence providing high assurance that a process/equipment/system consistently gives results meeting predetermined specifications.
Types: prospective (before release of new product), concurrent (during routine production), retrospective (from past batch data), revalidation (after changes or periodically).
Areas: process, cleaning, analytical method, equipment qualification (DQ, IQ, OQ, PQ), utilities, computer systems.
Calibration concerns instrument accuracy; validation concerns process consistency.
questions.question: Define calibration and validation. Write the types of validation.

questions.answer:
Testing raw and packing materials against specifications.
In-process control (weight, hardness, disintegration, pH, volume).
Finished product testing and release recommendation.
Stability studies, retention samples.
Environmental monitoring of clean areas.
Calibration of lab instruments and record keeping.
questions.question: Write the functions of the quality control department.

questions.answer:
Preparing and controlling SOPs and documents.
Reviewing batch records and releasing batches.
Training staff.
Audits, self-inspection, vendor approval.
Deviation, change control, complaints and recalls.
Overseeing validation and calibration.
questions.question: Write the functions of the quality assurance department.

questions.answer:
Adequate number of qualified and experienced staff.
Training in GMP and own duties.
Medical examination; sick persons kept away.
Personal hygiene; proper gowns, caps, masks, gloves.
No eating, drinking or smoking in production areas.
questions.question: Write the GMP requirements for personnel.

questions.answer:
Grade A – critical aseptic operations (filling, open sterile containers) under laminar air flow.
Grade B – background for Grade A.
Grade C and D – less critical steps such as solution preparation and component handling.
HEPA-filtered air, air locks, gowning.
questions.question: Write a short note on clean area grades.

questions.answer: Schedule M.
questions.question: Which schedule of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules deals with GMP?

questions.answer: Stages of equipment qualification: design, installation, operational and performance qualification.
questions.question: What are DQ, IQ, OQ and PQ?

questions.answer:
Definition: newer delivery approaches that control the rate, duration or site of drug release for better efficacy and safety.
By route: oral controlled release (matrix, reservoir, osmotic OROS – nifedipine; metformin ER); gastroretentive (floating); transdermal (nitroglycerin, nicotine, fentanyl, scopolamine, estradiol); ocular (Ocusert pilocarpine); intrauterine (levonorgestrel system); implants (levonorgestrel, etonogestrel, goserelin); mucoadhesive buccal; pulmonary (MDI, DPI); parenteral depots (microsphere injections).
By mechanism: diffusion (reservoir, matrix), dissolution, osmotic, ion-exchange, biodegradable, stimulus-responsive.
Targeted carriers: liposomes (liposomal amphotericin B, doxorubicin), niosomes, nanoparticles, microspheres, antibody conjugates, resealed erythrocytes; passive and active targeting.
questions.question: Define novel drug delivery systems. Classify them with examples.

questions.answer:
Advantages: fewer doses – better compliance; steady blood level within therapeutic window; fewer side effects and lower total dose; improved bioavailability, avoids first-pass (transdermal, buccal, implant); protects sensitive drugs; better control of chronic disease and night-time symptoms; targeting of anticancer drugs; removable systems (patch, implant).
Challenges: high cost; dose dumping if system fails (crushing, chewing); fixed dose, little flexibility; toxicity cannot be stopped quickly; unsuitable for drugs with very short/long half-life, large dose, poor absorption; variable GI transit; skin irritation from patches; complex manufacture and stability problems (liposome leakage); need for patient education; strict regulatory studies.
questions.question: Write the advantages and challenges of novel drug delivery systems.

questions.answer:
TDDS: patches delivering drug through skin into blood at a controlled rate. Structure – backing layer, drug reservoir/matrix, rate-controlling membrane, adhesive, release liner. Suitable drugs: potent, low dose, low molecular weight, suitable solubility. Examples: nitroglycerin, nicotine, fentanyl, scopolamine, estradiol. Merits: avoid first-pass, steady levels, removable. Demerits: skin irritation, limited drugs.
Osmotic pump (OROS): drug + osmotic agent core, semipermeable coat with laser-drilled orifice; water enters, builds osmotic pressure, pushes drug solution out at near zero-order rate independent of pH and food; e.g. nifedipine; empty shell passes in stools.
questions.question: Write notes on transdermal drug delivery systems and osmotic pumps.

questions.answer:
Draw blood level vs time: conventional doses show peaks above and troughs below the therapeutic window; controlled release keeps a steady level.
Terms: sustained release (slow, prolonged), controlled release (predetermined, often zero-order), zero-order vs first-order release.
Mechanisms: reservoir, matrix, dissolution, osmotic, ion-exchange, biodegradable.
Targeted delivery: carrier takes drug to target; passive (tumours with leaky vessels, liver/spleen uptake) and active (antibody or ligand on carrier). Carriers: liposomes, niosomes, nanoparticles, microspheres, antibody–drug conjugates, prodrugs (levodopa).
questions.question: Explain controlled release and targeted drug delivery with a diagram of blood levels.

questions.answer:
Vesicles of phospholipid bilayers (with cholesterol) around an aqueous core.
Water-soluble drug in core, lipid-soluble in bilayer.
Uses: targeting, reduced toxicity – liposomal amphotericin B, liposomal doxorubicin.
Demerits: cost, leakage, stability problems.
questions.question: Write a note on liposomes.

questions.answer:
Transdermal nitroglycerin/nicotine patch.
Ocusert – pilocarpine ocular insert.
OROS osmotic tablet – nifedipine.
Levonorgestrel implant or intrauterine system.
Liposomal amphotericin B.
questions.question: Give four examples of novel drug delivery systems with the drug used.

questions.answer: Sudden release of a large part or all of the dose from a modified-release product because the release mechanism fails (crushing, chewing, sometimes alcohol), which may cause toxicity.
questions.question: What is dose dumping?

questions.answer:
Sustained: drug released slowly over a prolonged period; rate not exactly controlled; level may decline slowly.
Controlled: drug released at a predetermined, often constant (zero-order) rate, giving steady levels.
questions.question: Differentiate between sustained release and controlled release.

questions.answer: An ocular insert placed in the eye that releases pilocarpine at a controlled rate for about a week.
questions.question: What is Ocusert?

units.markdown:
# Unit 1: History of pharmacy in India and pharmacopoeias

This unit covers syllabus chapter 1: how the pharmacy profession grew in India (education, industry, practice and professional bodies), pharmacy as a career, and the official books of standards called pharmacopoeias.

## 1.1 What pharmacy is

**Pharmacy** is the art and science of preparing, compounding, preserving, testing and dispensing medicines, and of advising patients on their safe use. The word comes from the Greek *pharmakon* (a drug or remedy).

A **pharmacist** is a person registered under the Pharmacy Act, 1948 with a State Pharmacy Council. Only a registered pharmacist may compound or dispense medicines on a prescription.

## 1.2 History of pharmacy in India

### Ancient and medieval period

- Indian systems of medicine (Ayurveda, Siddha and later Unani) had their own medicine makers. *Charaka Samhita* and *Sushruta Samhita* describe the collection, processing and preparation of herbal, mineral and animal drugs.
- In these systems the physician (vaidya or hakim) usually prepared and gave the medicine himself. Pharmacy was not a separate profession.

### British period

- Modern (allopathic) medicine came with the British. Medicines were imported, and the first chemist shops were set up in the port cities. Bathgate and Co. opened in Calcutta in 1811 and is often quoted as one of the earliest such shops.
- Hospital "compounders" were trained on the job. They had no formal education and no legal status.
- **Acharya P. C. Ray** founded **Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works** in Calcutta (registered as a company in 1901). It is regarded as the beginning of the Indian pharmaceutical industry.
- **Drugs Enquiry Committee (Chopra Committee), 1930–31**, chaired by Col. R. N. Chopra, studied the poor quality of drugs sold in India. It recommended a law to control drug quality, a national pharmacopoeia and proper training and registration of pharmacists.

### Laws that shaped the profession

| Year | Law or event | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1940 | Drugs Act (now Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940) | Controls import, manufacture, sale and distribution of drugs |
| 1946 | Indian Pharmacopoeial List | First Indian list of drug standards, before the first IP |
| 1948 | Pharmacy Act | Regulates the profession and pharmacy education |
| 1949 | Pharmacy Council of India (PCI) set up | Sets minimum standards of education; approves institutions |
| 1955 | First Indian Pharmacopoeia | Official Indian standards for drugs |
| 1985 | Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act | Control of habit-forming drugs |

### Pharmacy education

- **Prof. M. L. Schroff** started a pharmacy course at **Banaras Hindu University in 1932**. He is called the *father of pharmacy education in India*.
- After the Pharmacy Act, the PCI framed **Education Regulations** for the Diploma in Pharmacy. The diploma was revised several times; the current one is **Education Regulations 2020 (ER-2020)**, a two-year course followed by a practical training period.
- Today the main courses are D.Pharm (diploma), B.Pharm (degree), M.Pharm, Pharm.D and Ph.D.

| Course | Duration | What it allows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| D.Pharm | 2 years + practical training | Registration as a pharmacist |
| B.Pharm | 4 years | Registration; industry, hospital, community work |
| Pharm.D | 6 years (including internship) | Clinical pharmacy practice |
| M.Pharm | 2 years after B.Pharm | Specialisation, teaching, research |

### Pharmaceutical industry

- Before independence most drugs were imported. After independence public sector units such as **Hindustan Antibiotics Ltd (Pimpri)** and **Indian Drugs and Pharmaceuticals Ltd (IDPL)** were set up to make antibiotics and bulk drugs.
- The **Indian Patents Act, 1970** recognised only process patents for medicines. Indian firms could make cheaper versions of new drugs by different processes, and the industry grew fast.
- India is now a major producer of generic medicines and vaccines and is often called the *pharmacy of the world*.

### Pharmacy practice

Pharmacy practice in India covers:

- **Community (retail) pharmacy:** dispensing on prescription, counselling, health awareness.
- **Hospital pharmacy:** purchase, storage and supply of medicines inside a hospital, drug information, formulary work.
- **Clinical pharmacy:** working with doctors on the ward to make therapy safe and effective.

The PCI's **Pharmacy Practice Regulations, 2015** describe the duties and standards for registered pharmacists.

## 1.3 Professional associations

Professional associations bring pharmacists together, run conferences and journals, and speak for the profession.

| Association | Main role |
| --- | --- |
| Indian Pharmaceutical Association (IPA) | Oldest national body of pharmacists; publishes the *Indian Journal of Pharmaceutical Sciences* |
| Indian Pharmaceutical Congress Association (IPCA) | Holds the yearly Indian Pharmaceutical Congress with member bodies |
| Association of Pharmaceutical Teachers of India (APTI) | Body of pharmacy teachers; works on education quality |
| Indian Hospital Pharmacists' Association (IHPA) | Hospital pharmacists |
| Indian Pharmacy Graduates' Association (IPGA) | Pharmacy graduates |
| All India Organisation of Chemists and Druggists (AIOCD) | Trade body of chemists and druggists (retail and wholesale) |
| State Pharmacy Councils | Register pharmacists in each state (statutory bodies, not voluntary associations) |

Internationally, the **International Pharmaceutical Federation (FIP)** links national pharmacy bodies.

## 1.4 Pharmacy as a career

A diploma holder can register as a pharmacist and work in many fields.

| Field | Typical jobs |
| --- | --- |
| Community pharmacy | Retail pharmacist, own medical store (with a drug licence) |
| Hospital | Hospital pharmacist, store in-charge |
| Government | Pharmacist in health centres, dispensaries, armed forces, railways |
| Industry | Production, packaging, quality control, stores |
| Marketing | Medical representative, sales |
| Wholesale and distribution | Wholesale drug business |
| Further study | B.Pharm (lateral entry to second year), then higher studies |
| Regulatory | Drug inspector (needs a degree as per rules) |

**Qualities of a good pharmacist:** honesty, accuracy, good communication with patients, up-to-date knowledge, and respect for the code of ethics.

## 1.5 Pharmacopoeia

### Definition

A **pharmacopoeia** is a legally recognised book of standards for drugs, published under the authority of a government. It gives the standards of identity, purity and strength of drugs and their formulations, and the methods to test them.

The word comes from Greek *pharmakon* (drug) and *poiein* (to make).

**Formulary vs pharmacopoeia:** a pharmacopoeia mainly gives *standards and tests*; a formulary mainly gives *formulas* of preparations and information for prescribing.

### Contents of a typical monograph

```text
Monograph (one drug or one preparation)
 ├── Name, chemical structure, molecular formula and weight
 ├── Definition and content limits (e.g. not less than 98.0% and not more than 101.0%)
 ├── Category (e.g. analgesic) and dose (in older editions)
 ├── Description and solubility
 ├── Identification tests
 ├── Tests for purity (limits of impurities, loss on drying, sulphated ash, heavy metals)
 ├── Assay (how much drug is present)
 └── Storage and labelling
```

### Indian Pharmacopoeia (IP)

- Published by the **Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (IPC), Ghaziabad**, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
- It is the official book of standards under the **Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940**. Drugs sold in India must meet IP standards.

| Edition | Year |
| --- | --- |
| 1st | 1955 (supplement 1960) |
| 2nd | 1966 |
| 3rd | 1985 |
| 4th | 1996 |
| 5th | 2007 |
| 6th | 2010 |
| 7th | 2014 |
| 8th | 2018 |
| 9th | 2022 |

**Salient features of the Indian Pharmacopoeia (recent editions):**

1. Published in more than one volume: general notices and general chapters (appendices) first, then monographs of drug substances, dosage forms, and special groups.
2. **General notices** explain how to read the book: terms like "about", "constant weight", storage words (cool place, room temperature), and solubility terms.
3. **General chapters (appendices)** give official test methods: disintegration, dissolution, uniformity of weight, sterility, pyrogen and bacterial endotoxin tests, limit tests, sieves and powder grades.
4. Monographs on **drug substances**, **dosage forms** (tablets, capsules, injections, etc.), **vaccines and immunological products**, **blood products**, **herbal products**, **radiopharmaceuticals** and **veterinary products**.
5. Uses **SI units** and modern instrumental methods (HPLC, UV, IR).
6. Doses and categories are usually not part of the monograph in recent editions; the IP is a book of standards, not a prescribing guide.
7. Updated by addenda between editions.

### Other important pharmacopoeias and references

| Book | Country / publisher | Key facts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| British Pharmacopoeia (BP) | UK; British Pharmacopoeia Commission | First edition 1864; now revised every year; includes European Pharmacopoeia monographs |
| United States Pharmacopeia (USP) | USA; United States Pharmacopeial Convention | First edition 1820; standards of drug substances and products |
| National Formulary (NF) | USA | First published in 1888 by the American Pharmaceutical Association; mainly excipients; combined with USP as **USP–NF** |
| Extra Pharmacopoeia (Martindale) | UK; Royal Pharmaceutical Society | First compiled by William Martindale in 1883; now *Martindale: The Complete Drug Reference*; gives information on almost all drugs used anywhere |
| International Pharmacopoeia (Ph. Int.) | World Health Organization | Standards for use mainly in developing countries |
| National Formulary of India (NFI) | India | Prescribing guide for doctors and pharmacists |

**Extra Pharmacopoeia is not an official book of standards.** It is a reference book: drug monographs with uses, doses, adverse effects, interactions and proprietary names from many countries.

## 1.6 Unit 1 summary map

```text
                     UNIT 1
  ┌──────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┐
HISTORY               CAREER                 PHARMACOPOEIA
• Ayurveda/Unani      • community, hospital  • definition: legal book of standards
• Bengal Chemical     • industry, marketing  • IP: IPC Ghaziabad, 1955 → 2022
• Chopra Cttee 1930   • govt, wholesale      • BP 1864, USP 1820, NF 1888
• Drugs Act 1940      • higher studies       • USP–NF combined
• Pharmacy Act 1948                          • Martindale = Extra Pharmacopoeia
• PCI 1949, ER-2020                          • monograph: identity, purity, assay
```

## Remember

- Pharmacy Act **1948**; PCI constituted **1949**; Drugs and Cosmetics Act **1940**.
- Father of pharmacy education in India: **Prof. M. L. Schroff** (BHU, 1932).
- Chopra Committee (1930–31) asked for drug laws, a national pharmacopoeia and trained pharmacists.
- First IP **1955**; current edition **IP 2022**, published by the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad.
- A pharmacopoeia gives *standards*; a formulary gives *formulas*; Martindale gives *information*.
- BP 1864, USP 1820, NF 1888; USP and NF are now published together.
